```{r}
root <- normalizePath("..")

outputs <- file.path(root, "03.outputs")

# The Python chunks run through reticulate on the MacPorts interpreter the
# retrieval and computation were written for.

# Write figures into the committed outputs folder rather than the render
# sidecar. With embed-resources the sidecar is deleted once its contents are
# inlined into the HTML, which leaves no PNG on disk for the README to show.
# Writing them here keeps a copy that survives the render and is in the
# repository.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = file.path("..", "03.outputs", "figures", "mfig-"), dev = c("png", "cairo_pdf"))

# House table format: 9 pt, centred headers, numeric right, text left, single
# line spacing. Every table goes through fmt_tbl, so the house style is defined
# once and cannot drift between tables. The two widest tables, set on landscape
# pages in the Word build on 2026-10-26, pass size = 8, and the trend table
# centres its numeric columns, both following Seamus's hand formatting that day.
fmt_tbl <- function(df, right = NULL, size = 9, numeric = "right") {
  right_cols <- union(names(df)[vapply(df, is.numeric, TRUE)], right)
  left_cols <- setdiff(names(df), right_cols)
  ft <- flextable::flextable(df)
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = size, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, align = "center", part = "header")
  if (length(right_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = right_cols, align = numeric, part = "body")
  if (length(left_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = left_cols, align = "left", part = "body")
  ft <- flextable::line_spacing(ft, space = 1, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::padding(ft, padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1, part = "all")
  flextable::set_table_properties(ft, layout = "autofit", width = 1)
}

# Read a value out of a two-column item/value table by name. Stops rather than
# returning empty, so a renamed row breaks the render instead of silently
# emptying a sentence.
lookup <- function(tbl, item) {
  v <- tbl$value[tbl$item == item]
  if (length(v) != 1) stop("no unique row for: ", item)
  v
}
n_fmt <- function(x) format(as.numeric(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)

# The three timeseries, named once. Everything downstream reads these labels rather
# than repeating them, so the version and the input resolution attached to a
# series cannot drift between a table and the sentence describing it.
SERIES <- c(s1 = "S1: FWI1987, 13:00 observation",
            s2 = "S2: FWI2025, 13:00 observation",
            s3 = "S3: FWI2025, hourly observation")
# The same three timeseries as they are named inside a sentence, where a table
# label with its code and colon would not read.
SERIES_PROSE <- c(s1 = "FWI1987 on the 13:00 observation",
                  s2 = "FWI2025 on the 13:00 observation",
                  s3 = "FWI2025 on hourly weather")
# Station names arrive from the data mart in capitals; prose uses title case,
# keeping the RS suffix (ranger station) as the service writes it.
station_prose <- function(x) {
  x <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(x))
  x <- gsub("\\bRs\\b", "RS", x)
  gsub("\\bMccuddy\\b", "McCuddy", x)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| output: false
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Statistical functions for forest-fire-index-trends.
##
## Written 2026-08-15. These are defined here and called from the chunks that
## follow, so that the manuscript carries the machinery it runs.
##
## Three things are done here and each carries a decision that has to be stated
## wherever a number from it is reported.
##
## Trend estimation. The estimator is the Theil-Sen slope, the median of all
## pairwise slopes, chosen because seasonal counts of extreme days are skewed and
## a least squares slope on them is pulled by single seasons. Significance is
## Mann-Kendall with the Hamed and Rao (1998) variance correction, which inflates
## the variance of the S statistic by the autocorrelation actually present in the
## series rather than assuming independence. Serial correlation in seasonal fire
## danger is real and untreated Mann-Kendall over-rejects in its presence, so the
## uncorrected test is reported alongside only to show the size of the effect.
##
## Slope differences between series. The three series are computed from one
## weather record, so they are strongly dependent and a two-sample test on their
## slopes is wrong. The difference is bootstrapped by resampling whole seasons
## with replacement, recomputing both slopes on the same resampled seasons each
## time. The pairing is preserved by construction, so the interval is on the
## difference and not on two separately noisy slopes.
##
## Multiple testing. A metric family is corrected within each series by the
## Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) false discovery rate procedure. The family is
## declared at the call site, not here, because what counts as one family is a
## judgement about the question and not about the arithmetic.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Theil-Sen slope with a Mann-Kendall test corrected for serial correlation.
##
## Returns one row: the slope, its bootstrap interval, the corrected and
## uncorrected p values, Kendall's tau, and the effective sample size ratio that
## the correction used. A series shorter than `min_n` returns NA rather than a
## number, because a slope over eight seasons is not an estimate.
## Moving-block bootstrap indices over an ordered season sequence.
##
## Resampling single seasons keeps the pairing between series that share a
## weather record but discards serial correlation within a series. Blocks of
## consecutive seasons keep it (Kunsch 1989). Block length is the cube root of
## the number of seasons, rounded up and at least two, which grows with the
## record but more slowly than it, as Kunsch's consistency condition requires.
## Blocks are drawn from the seasons in order of occurrence, so a gap in the
## record falls inside a block rather than being closed up.
block_length <- function(n) max(2L, as.integer(ceiling(n^(1/3))))
block_indices <- function(n, l = block_length(n)) {
  starts <- sample.int(n - l + 1L, ceiling(n / l), replace = TRUE)
  idx <- as.vector(vapply(starts, function(s) s:(s + l - 1L), integer(l)))
  idx[seq_len(n)]
}

trend_test <- function(year, value, min_n = 15, n_boot = 2000, seed = 20260815) {
  ok <- is.finite(year) & is.finite(value)
  year <- year[ok]; value <- value[ok]
  o <- order(year); year <- year[o]; value <- value[o]
  n <- length(value)

  na_row <- data.frame(n = n, slope = NA_real_, lower = NA_real_, upper = NA_real_,
                       p_corrected = NA_real_, p_uncorrected = NA_real_,
                       tau = NA_real_, n_over_nstar = NA_real_)
  if (n < min_n || length(unique(value)) < 3) return(na_row)

  mk <- tryCatch(modifiedmk::mmkh(as.vector(value)), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(mk)) return(na_row)

  ## Theil-Sen on the actual years, so a gap in the season sequence is honoured
  ## rather than treated as a step of one.
  slope <- theil_sen(year, value)

  set.seed(seed)
  bs <- vapply(seq_len(n_boot), function(i) {
    k <- block_indices(n)
    theil_sen(year[k], value[k])
  }, numeric(1))

  data.frame(
    n = n,
    slope = slope,
    lower = unname(quantile(bs, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)),
    upper = unname(quantile(bs, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)),
    p_corrected = unname(mk["new P-value"]),
    p_uncorrected = unname(mk["old P.value"]),
    tau = unname(mk["Tau"]),
    n_over_nstar = unname(mk["N/N*"])
  )
}

## Median of all pairwise slopes. Returns NA when fewer than two distinct x
## values survive, which happens inside a bootstrap resample.
##
## Written with outer() rather than an index expansion because the bootstraps
## above call it several hundred thousand times and the allocation cost of
## building index vectors on every call dominated the runtime.
theil_sen <- function(x, y) {
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 3) return(NA_real_)
  dx <- outer(x, x, "-")
  dy <- outer(y, y, "-")
  keep <- lower.tri(dx) & dx != 0
  if (!any(keep)) return(NA_real_)
  median(dy[keep] / dx[keep])
}

## Paired bootstrap on the difference between two series' Theil-Sen slopes.
##
## `wide` must hold one row per season with columns `year`, `a` and `b`. Seasons
## are resampled whole, so both slopes are recomputed on the same seasons in
## every replicate and the dependence between the series is carried through.
slope_difference <- function(wide, n_boot = 4000, seed = 20260815) {
  wide <- wide[is.finite(wide$a) & is.finite(wide$b), ]
  n <- nrow(wide)
  if (n < 15) {
    return(data.frame(n = n, slope_a = NA_real_, slope_b = NA_real_,
                      difference = NA_real_, lower = NA_real_, upper = NA_real_,
                      p_two_sided = NA_real_))
  }
  sa <- theil_sen(wide$year, wide$a)
  sb <- theil_sen(wide$year, wide$b)

  wide <- wide[order(wide$year), ]
  set.seed(seed)
  d <- vapply(seq_len(n_boot), function(i) {
    k <- block_indices(n)
    theil_sen(wide$year[k], wide$b[k]) - theil_sen(wide$year[k], wide$a[k])
  }, numeric(1))
  d <- d[is.finite(d)]

  ## Two sided bootstrap p value computed under the null hypothesis, following
  ## the first guideline of Hall and Wilson (1991): the resampled differences
  ## are centred on the observed difference, and p is the share whose distance
  ## from it is at least as large as the observed difference is from zero,
  ## floored at the resolution the number of replicates can resolve.
  obs <- sb - sa
  p <- mean(abs(d - obs) >= abs(obs))
  data.frame(
    n = n, slope_a = sa, slope_b = sb, difference = sb - sa,
    lower = unname(quantile(d, 0.025)), upper = unname(quantile(d, 0.975)),
    p_two_sided = max(p, 1 / length(d))
  )
}

## Benjamini and Hochberg false discovery rate over a declared family.
fdr <- function(p) p.adjust(p, method = "BH")

## Negative binomial count model of daily ignitions on daily fire danger.
##
## Season is a factor, so the danger coefficient is identified only from
## day-to-day variation inside a season. That is deliberate. Reporting
## completeness and cause coding both change between seasons and neither changes
## within one, so a between-season contrast would confound the danger effect with
## the record keeping, and a within-season contrast cannot.
##
## Day of year enters as a pair of annual harmonics, which absorbs the seasonal
## march of both fuel dryness and human activity without spending a parameter per
## day.
ignition_model <- function(d, response, danger, extra = NULL) {
  d <- d[is.finite(d[[danger]]) & is.finite(d[[response]]), ]
  d$.y <- d[[response]]
  d$.x <- d[[danger]]
  d$.s1 <- sin(2 * pi * d$doy / 365.25); d$.c1 <- cos(2 * pi * d$doy / 365.25)
  d$.s2 <- sin(4 * pi * d$doy / 365.25); d$.c2 <- cos(4 * pi * d$doy / 365.25)
  d$.year <- factor(d$year)
  f <- ".y ~ .x + .s1 + .c1 + .s2 + .c2 + .year"
  if (!is.null(extra)) f <- paste(f, "+", extra)
  MASS::glm.nb(as.formula(f), data = d, control = glm.control(maxit = 100))
}

## Out of sample predictive skill, by leaving one season out at a time.
##
## Returns the mean held-out log likelihood per day under the negative binomial
## fitted without that season. Comparing series on held-out likelihood rather
## than on in-sample fit is the point: three series computed from one weather
## record will all fit, and the question is which predicts.
loso_skill <- function(d, response, danger, extra = "n_stations") {
  years <- sort(unique(d$year))
  ll <- numeric(0)
  ## A coefficient can come back NA when its term is collinear inside a training
  ## fold; treating it as zero keeps the fold rather than dropping it silently.
  cf <- function(co, nm) if (nm %in% names(co) && is.finite(co[[nm]])) co[[nm]] else 0

  for (y in years) {
    train <- d[d$year != y, ]
    test <- d[d$year == y, ]
    if (nrow(test) < 30 || length(unique(train$year)) < 5) next
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(train, response, danger, extra = extra),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    ## The held-out season has no fitted year effect, so prediction uses the mean
    ## of the fitted year effects: the model is asked for a typical season, which
    ## is what a forecast for an unobserved season can know.
    co <- coef(m)
    yr_terms <- co[grepl("^\\.year", names(co))]
    eta <- cf(co, "(Intercept)") + mean(c(0, yr_terms), na.rm = TRUE) +
      cf(co, ".x") * test[[danger]] +
      cf(co, ".s1") * sin(2 * pi * test$doy / 365.25) +
      cf(co, ".c1") * cos(2 * pi * test$doy / 365.25) +
      cf(co, ".s2") * sin(4 * pi * test$doy / 365.25) +
      cf(co, ".c2") * cos(4 * pi * test$doy / 365.25)
    if (!is.null(extra) && extra == "n_stations")
      eta <- eta + cf(co, "n_stations") * test$n_stations
    mu <- exp(eta)
    ll <- c(ll, dnbinom(test[[response]], size = m$theta, mu = mu, log = TRUE))
  }
  if (!length(ll)) return(data.frame(n_days = 0L, mean_loglik = NA_real_,
                                     total_loglik = NA_real_))
  data.frame(n_days = length(ll), mean_loglik = mean(ll), total_loglik = sum(ll))
}

## Minimum trend a window of n seasons can detect, at the observed noise level.
##
## Solves for the slope at which a Mann-Kendall test would reject at alpha with
## power 1 - beta, given the residual standard deviation of the series about its
## own Theil-Sen line. This is the quantitative form of what a 35 season window
## cannot resolve, and it is computed rather than asserted.
minimum_detectable_trend <- function(year, value, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.9) {
  ok <- is.finite(year) & is.finite(value)
  year <- year[ok]; value <- value[ok]
  n <- length(value)
  if (n < 10) return(NA_real_)
  s <- theil_sen(year, value)
  resid <- value - (s * (year - mean(year)) + median(value - s * (year - mean(year))))
  sigma <- sd(resid)
  ## Standard error of an ordinary least squares slope is the relevant scale;
  ## Theil-Sen is about 93 per cent as efficient as least squares under normal
  ## errors, so the result is divided by that efficiency to stay honest.
  se <- sigma / sqrt(sum((year - mean(year))^2))
  ## Serial correlation inflates the standard error of a trend by
  ## sqrt((1 + phi) / (1 - phi)) for first-order autoregressive noise with lag-one
  ## autocorrelation phi (Weatherhead et al. 1998). phi is estimated from the
  ## residuals in season order and bounded to [0, 0.9], so that a negative sample
  ## estimate cannot shrink the detectable trend below the independent case.
  r <- resid[order(year)]
  phi <- if (length(r) > 2) suppressWarnings(stats::cor(r[-1], r[-length(r)])) else 0
  phi <- min(max(ifelse(is.finite(phi), phi, 0), 0), 0.9)
  (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power)) * se * sqrt((1 + phi) / (1 - phi)) / 0.93
}


## Percentile exceedance counts with the in-base bootstrap correction of Zhang,
## Hegerl, Zwiers and Kenyon (2005).
##
## A threshold estimated from a fixed base period carries sampling error that
## biases counts low inside the base period and high outside it, which a trend
## fitted across the boundary reads as a trend. Zhang et al. removed the jump by
## estimating the count for each in-base year from thresholds that exclude that
## year. For each in-base season j, the base sample is rebuilt with season j
## removed and another base season i duplicated in its place, the threshold is
## re-estimated, and the count in season j is taken; the count for j is the mean
## over every i other than j. Out-of-base seasons use the threshold from the whole
## base period. Zhang et al. estimated calendar-day thresholds; here, as in the
## uncorrected metric, the threshold is estimated from all days of the season
## pooled, so the procedure is adapted to a seasonal rather than daily threshold.
## Quantiles use type 7, the numpy default the uncorrected metric used, and the
## comparison is strictly greater than, as in the uncorrected metric.
inbase_corrected_counts <- function(daily, series, probs = c(90, 95),
                                    reference = c(1991, 2020), min_ref = 500,
                                    component = "fwi") {
  col <- paste0(series, "_", component)
  out <- list()
  for (stn in unique(daily$station_name)) {
    g <- daily[daily$station_name == stn & is.finite(daily[[col]]), c("year", col)]
    names(g)[2] <- "v"
    by_year <- split(g$v, g$year)
    years <- as.integer(names(by_year))
    base <- years[years >= reference[1] & years <= reference[2]]
    base_vals <- unlist(by_year[as.character(base)], use.names = FALSE)
    for (p in probs) {
      if (length(base_vals) < min_ref) {
        cnt <- rep(NA_real_, length(years))
      } else {
        full <- unname(stats::quantile(base_vals, p / 100, type = 7))
        cnt <- vapply(years, function(y) {
          v <- by_year[[as.character(y)]]
          if (!(y %in% base)) return(sum(v > full))
          others <- setdiff(base, y)
          without <- unlist(by_year[as.character(others)], use.names = FALSE)
          mean(vapply(others, function(i) {
            thr <- stats::quantile(c(without, by_year[[as.character(i)]]), p / 100,
                                   type = 7, names = FALSE)
            sum(v > thr)
          }, numeric(1)))
        }, numeric(1))
      }
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- data.frame(station_name = stn, series = series,
                                           year = years, prob = p, count = cnt)
    }
  }
  do.call(rbind, out)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: resolve-study-area-boundary
#| output: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Which official boundary is "the entire Okanagan watershed"?
#
# Written 2026-08-14, on Seamus's instruction to settle the study area from
# official government geographic data rather than from the identifier the
# framing document carried. The framing named Freshwater Atlas identifier 212,
# which is Turnagain River in the far north of the province and cannot be what
# was meant.
#
# Three official definitions exist and they disagree by a factor of two, so the
# choice has to be made on evidence rather than on the first layer that returns
# a polygon named Okanagan. This script retrieves all three, measures them, and
# measures what the differences between them consist of. Every number the
# framing document and the review protocol quote about the study-area ruling is
# computed here.
#
#   1. WHSE_BASEMAPPING.FWA_WATERSHED_GROUPS_POLY, WATERSHED_GROUP_ID 161, code
#      OKAN. The Freshwater Atlas is the province's authoritative hydrological
#      framework at 1:20,000.
#   2. WHSE_BASEMAPPING.BC_MAJOR_WATERSHEDS, MAJOR_WATERSHED_CODE WA2, named
#      "Okanagan River".
#   3. WHSE_IMAGERY_AND_BASE_MAPS.DRP_SUB_SUB_DRAINAGES_1M_SP, sub-sub-drainage
#      08NM, named "Okanagan". This is the federal Standard Drainage Area
#      Classification of the Water Survey of Canada, generalised to 1:1,000,000
#      and independent of the provincial framework.
#
# Nothing here computes an outcome. It measures polygons.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The comparison is planar in BC Albers over areas of a few thousand square
# kilometres, where the projection is the appropriate measurement surface and
# s2's spherical predicates only introduce edge cases on the boundary overlaps.
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

CRS_WORK <- 3005                    # NAD83 / BC Albers, metric, per framing

derived_dir <- file.path(root, "02.inputs", "derived")
boundary_csv <- file.path(derived_dir, "study-area-boundary-candidates.csv")

WFS <- "https://openmaps.gov.bc.ca/geo/pub/wfs"

wfs_get <- function(layer, cql = NULL, page = 10000) {
  q <- c(service = "WFS", version = "2.0.0", request = "GetFeature",
         typeName = layer, outputFormat = "application/json",
         srsName = paste0("EPSG:", CRS_WORK), count = page)
  url <- paste0(WFS, "?", paste0(names(q), "=",
                                 vapply(q, utils::URLencode, "", reserved = TRUE),
                                 collapse = "&"))
  if (!is.null(cql))
    url <- paste0(url, "&CQL_FILTER=", utils::URLencode(cql, reserved = TRUE))
  sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_read(url, quiet = TRUE))
}

ha <- function(x) as.numeric(sum(sf::st_area(x))) / 1e4
msg <- function(...) cat(sprintf(...), "\n")

if (!file.exists(boundary_csv)) {
# --- The three candidates --------------------------------------------------
# Freshwater Atlas Watershed Groups, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/freshwater-atlas-watershed-groups
fwa <- wfs_get("WHSE_BASEMAPPING.FWA_WATERSHED_GROUPS_POLY",
               "WATERSHED_GROUP_ID=161")
# BC Major Watersheds, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/bc-major-watersheds
bcmw <- wfs_get("WHSE_BASEMAPPING.BC_MAJOR_WATERSHEDS",
                "MAJOR_WATERSHED_SYSTEM LIKE '%kanagan%'")
# Water Survey of Canada Sub-Sub-Drainage Areas, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/water-survey-of-canada-sub-sub-drainage-areas
wsc <- wfs_get("WHSE_IMAGERY_AND_BASE_MAPS.DRP_SUB_SUB_DRAINAGES_1M_SP",
               "SUB_SUB_DRAINAGE_AREA_CD='08NM'")
# Freshwater Atlas Watershed Groups, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/freshwater-atlas-watershed-groups
groups <- wfs_get("WHSE_BASEMAPPING.FWA_WATERSHED_GROUPS_POLY")
# Province of British Columbia, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/province-of-british-columbia-legally-defined-administrative-areas-of-bc
prov <- wfs_get("WHSE_LEGAL_ADMIN_BOUNDARIES.ABMS_PROVINCE_SP")

msg("FWA watershed group 161 OKAN   %10.0f ha", ha(fwa))
msg("BC major watershed WA2         %10.0f ha", ha(bcmw))
msg("WSC sub-sub-drainage 08NM      %10.0f ha", ha(wsc))

# --- What BC's major watershed adds ----------------------------------------
# Decomposing WA2 against the Freshwater Atlas groups, rather than eyeballing
# the polygon, is what identifies the extra basin by name.
decompose <- function(target, label) {
  ix <- suppressWarnings(sf::st_intersection(groups, sf::st_union(target)))
  ix$ha <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(ix)) / 1e4
  ix$frac <- ix$ha / groups$AREA_HA[match(ix$WATERSHED_GROUP_ID,
                                          groups$WATERSHED_GROUP_ID)]
  ix <- ix[ix$frac > 0.01, ]
  ix <- ix[order(-ix$ha), ]
  msg("\nFreshwater Atlas groups making up %s:", label)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(ix)))
    msg("  %-20s %9.0f ha  %5.1f%% of that group",
        ix$WATERSHED_GROUP_NAME[i], ix$ha[i], 100 * ix$frac[i])
  ix
}
wa2_parts <- decompose(bcmw, "BC major watershed WA2 Okanagan River")
nm_parts <- decompose(wsc, "WSC sub-sub-drainage 08NM Okanagan")

# --- Where the federal unit's excess lies ----------------------------------
# 08NM is larger than the Freshwater Atlas group. The question is whether that
# excess is Canadian drainage the provincial group omits, which would matter, or
# the United States portion of the basin, which does not, because the ignition
# record and the fire weather network are both provincial.
resid <- suppressWarnings(sf::st_difference(sf::st_union(wsc), sf::st_union(fwa)))
resid_bc <- suppressWarnings(sf::st_intersection(resid, sf::st_union(prov)))
resid_ha <- ha(resid)
resid_bc_ha <- ha(resid_bc)
msg("\n08NM outside the Freshwater Atlas group: %.0f ha", resid_ha)
msg("  inside British Columbia:  %8.0f ha", resid_bc_ha)
msg("  outside British Columbia: %8.0f ha", resid_ha - resid_bc_ha)

ll <- sf::st_bbox(sf::st_transform(wsc, 4326))
msg("08NM southern limit: %.3f degrees north (the border is 49.000)", ll["ymin"])

# --- Record ----------------------------------------------------------------
similkameen <- wa2_parts$ha[wa2_parts$WATERSHED_GROUP_NAME == "Similkameen River"]
out <- data.frame(
  item = c("fwa_okan_ha", "bcmw_wa2_ha", "wsc_08nm_ha",
           "wa2_similkameen_ha", "nm_outside_fwa_ha", "nm_outside_fwa_in_bc_ha",
           "nm_outside_fwa_outside_bc_ha", "nm_south_limit_deg",
           "agreement_fwa_vs_wsc_in_bc_pct"),
  value = c(round(ha(fwa)), round(ha(bcmw)), round(ha(wsc)),
            round(if (length(similkameen)) similkameen else NA_real_),
            round(resid_ha), round(resid_bc_ha), round(resid_ha - resid_bc_ha),
            round(as.numeric(ll["ymin"]), 3),
            round(100 * resid_bc_ha / ha(fwa), 2)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
write.csv(out, boundary_csv, row.names = FALSE)
msg("\nWritten 02.inputs/derived/study-area-boundary-candidates.csv")
}

# --- The ruling this evidence supports --------------------------------------
# Recorded here so the reasoning sits beside the numbers rather than only in the
# framing document.
#
# BC's major watershed WA2 is the Freshwater Atlas Okanagan group plus the
# Similkameen group. The two are joined in that layer because the Similkameen
# reaches the Okanogan River in Washington State, not because the Similkameen
# drains to Okanagan Lake. It is a separate valley with its own climate and its
# own fire regime, and no ordinary use of "the Okanagan watershed" includes it.
#
# The federal unit 08NM is the whole binational basin. Almost all of its excess
# over the Freshwater Atlas group is south of the international boundary. Within
# Canada the two frameworks describe the same basin, differing by about one per
# cent, which is what a 1:1,000,000 generalisation costs against 1:20,000.
#
# The study area is therefore Freshwater Atlas watershed group 161, OKAN,
# Okanagan River: the Canadian portion of the Okanagan watershed, entire. The
# United States portion is excluded because the ignition record is the BC
# Wildfire Service historical incident layer and the validation weather is the
# BC Fire Weather Network, neither of which crosses the border. That exclusion
# is a stated boundary of the study, not an oversight.
```

```{r}
#| label: fetch-study-area
#| output: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Study area layers for the located methods figure.
#
# Written 2026-08-14. Retrieves every layer the study-area map draws, from the
# BC Data Catalogue WFS and the AWS terrain tiles, and writes them to one
# GeoPackage with a checksum manifest. Nothing is hand-digitised and nothing is
# hand-placed: every feature on the map comes from a named public layer that
# this script fetched, so the figure regenerates from code alone.
#
# Study area. Settled 2026-08-14 by Seamus's ruling that the study area is the
# entire Okanagan watershed as official government data defines it. The framing
# document had named "Freshwater Atlas identifier 212", which is Turnagain River
# in the far north and cannot have been meant.
#
# Three official boundaries carry the name and they disagree by a factor of two.
# The chunk above retrieves and measures all three, and
# writes 02.inputs/derived/study-area-boundary-candidates.csv. Its finding: BC's
# major watershed WA2 "Okanagan River", 1,554,467 ha, is this group plus the
# Similkameen, joined only because the Similkameen reaches the Okanogan River in
# Washington; and the federal Water Survey of Canada sub-sub-drainage 08NM,
# 1,203,045 ha, is the whole binational basin, 402,172 ha of it south of the
# border. Within Canada the federal and provincial frameworks agree to 10,327
# ha, 1.3 per cent.
#
# The study area is therefore WATERSHED_GROUP_ID 161, code OKAN, Okanagan River,
# 795,417 ha: the Canadian portion of the Okanagan watershed, entire. The United
# States portion is excluded because neither the BC Wildfire Service incident
# record nor the BC Fire Weather Network crosses the border, and that exclusion
# is a stated boundary of the study.
#
# Nothing here computes an outcome. It retrieves geometry and counts features.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

GROUP_ID <- 161                     # FWA watershed group, Okanagan River
FIRST_YEAR <- 1980                  # Framing: 1980 to 2025 fire seasons
LAST_YEAR <- 2025
CRS_WORK <- 3005                    # NAD83 / BC Albers, metric, per framing

spatial_dir <- file.path(root, "02.inputs", "spatial")
derived_dir <- file.path(root, "02.inputs", "derived")
dir.create(spatial_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
gpkg <- file.path(spatial_dir, "study-area.gpkg")

WFS <- "https://openmaps.gov.bc.ca/geo/pub/wfs"

# The service caps a response at 10,000 features, so every call pages by
# startIndex until a page comes back short. A silent truncation here would put
# the wrong ignition count on the figure, which is exactly the kind of number
# that never gets questioned once it is drawn.
wfs_get <- function(layer, cql = NULL, page = 5000) {
  out <- list()
  start <- 0
  repeat {
    q <- c(service = "WFS", version = "2.0.0", request = "GetFeature",
           typeName = layer, outputFormat = "application/json",
           srsName = paste0("EPSG:", CRS_WORK), count = page,
           startIndex = start)
    url <- paste0(WFS, "?", paste0(names(q), "=", vapply(q, utils::URLencode,
                                                         "", reserved = TRUE),
                                   collapse = "&"))
    if (!is.null(cql))
      url <- paste0(url, "&CQL_FILTER=", utils::URLencode(cql, reserved = TRUE))
    got <- sf::st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
    out[[length(out) + 1]] <- got
    if (nrow(got) < page) break
    start <- start + page
  }
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

msg <- function(...) cat(sprintf(...), "\n")

if (!file.exists(gpkg)) {
# --- Basin -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Freshwater Atlas Watershed Groups, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/freshwater-atlas-watershed-groups
basin <- wfs_get("WHSE_BASEMAPPING.FWA_WATERSHED_GROUPS_POLY",
                 sprintf("WATERSHED_GROUP_ID=%d", GROUP_ID))
stopifnot(nrow(basin) == 1)
msg("Basin: %s (%s), %.0f ha", basin$WATERSHED_GROUP_NAME,
    basin$WATERSHED_GROUP_CODE, basin$AREA_HA)
bb <- sf::st_bbox(basin)
bbox_cql <- sprintf("BBOX(SHAPE,%f,%f,%f,%f,'EPSG:%d')",
                    bb["xmin"], bb["ymin"], bb["xmax"], bb["ymax"], CRS_WORK)

# --- Ignitions -------------------------------------------------------------
# Retrieved on the bounding box, then clipped to the basin polygon, because the
# WFS spatial filter is a rectangle. The clip is what the count reports.
# BC Wildfire Fire Incident Locations, Historical, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/bc-wildfire-fire-incident-locations-historical
inc <- wfs_get("WHSE_LAND_AND_NATURAL_RESOURCE.PROT_HISTORICAL_INCIDENTS_SP",
               sprintf("%s AND FIRE_YEAR>=%d AND FIRE_YEAR<=%d",
                       bbox_cql, FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR))
msg("Incidents in bounding box, %d to %d: %d", FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR, nrow(inc))
inc <- inc[lengths(sf::st_intersects(inc, basin)) > 0, ]
msg("Incidents inside the basin: %d", nrow(inc))

# --- Landscape features ----------------------------------------------------
# Freshwater Atlas Lakes, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/freshwater-atlas-lakes
lakes <- wfs_get("WHSE_BASEMAPPING.FWA_LAKES_POLY",
                 sprintf("WATERSHED_GROUP_ID=%d AND AREA_HA>100", GROUP_ID))
lakes <- lakes[lengths(sf::st_intersects(lakes, basin)) > 0, ]
msg("Lakes over 100 ha: %d, of which named: %d", nrow(lakes),
    sum(!is.na(lakes$GNIS_NAME_1)))

# Freshwater Atlas Stream Network, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/freshwater-atlas-stream-network
streams <- wfs_get("WHSE_BASEMAPPING.FWA_STREAM_NETWORKS_SP",
                   sprintf("WATERSHED_GROUP_ID=%d AND STREAM_ORDER>=5",
                           GROUP_ID))
msg("Stream segments of order 5 or greater: %d", nrow(streams))

# --- Placenames ------------------------------------------------------------
# Municipal boundaries carry the authoritative name; the label goes on the
# centroid. BCGN geographical names is not served on this endpoint.
# Municipalities, Legally Defined Administrative Areas of BC, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/municipalities-legally-defined-administrative-areas-of-bc
munis <- wfs_get("WHSE_LEGAL_ADMIN_BOUNDARIES.ABMS_MUNICIPALITIES_SP",
                 bbox_cql)
munis <- munis[lengths(sf::st_intersects(munis, basin)) > 0, ]
places <- sf::st_centroid(sf::st_geometry(munis))
places <- sf::st_sf(name = munis$ADMIN_AREA_NAME,
                    type = munis$ADMIN_AREA_BOUNDARY_TYPE,
                    geometry = places)
msg("Municipalities intersecting the basin: %d", nrow(places))

# --- Weather ---------------------------------------------------------------
# BC Fire Weather Network stations. The framing names these as the validation
# source for whatever gridded product is adopted at the design gate.
# BC Wildfire Active Weather Stations, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/bc-wildfire-active-weather-stations
stations <- wfs_get("WHSE_LAND_AND_NATURAL_RESOURCE.PROT_WEATHER_STATIONS_SP",
                    bbox_cql)
stations <- stations[lengths(sf::st_intersects(stations, basin)) > 0, ]
msg("Fire weather stations inside the basin: %d", nrow(stations))

# ERA5-Land grid, the leading candidate weather input. Its cells are a fixed
# 0.1 degree geographic graticule, so the geometry is constructed rather than
# downloaded: drawing it states the support at which a candidate climate input
# would be resolved, which is the point of putting it on a methods map. No
# ERA5-Land values are retrieved, because the weather source is not settled.
b_ll <- sf::st_bbox(sf::st_transform(basin, 4326))
gx <- seq(floor(b_ll["xmin"] * 10) / 10, ceiling(b_ll["xmax"] * 10) / 10, 0.1)
gy <- seq(floor(b_ll["ymin"] * 10) / 10, ceiling(b_ll["ymax"] * 10) / 10, 0.1)
era5 <- sf::st_as_sf(sf::st_make_grid(
  sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(c(xmin = min(gx), ymin = min(gy),
                              xmax = max(gx), ymax = max(gy)),
                            crs = 4326)),
  cellsize = 0.1, offset = c(min(gx), min(gy))))
names(era5)[1] <- "geometry"
sf::st_geometry(era5) <- "geometry"
era5 <- sf::st_transform(era5, CRS_WORK)
era5 <- era5[lengths(sf::st_intersects(era5, basin)) > 0, ]
msg("ERA5-Land 0.1 degree cells intersecting the basin: %d", nrow(era5))

# --- Province, for the inset -----------------------------------------------
# Province of British Columbia, https://catalogue.data.gov.bc.ca/dataset/province-of-british-columbia-legally-defined-administrative-areas-of-bc
prov <- wfs_get("WHSE_LEGAL_ADMIN_BOUNDARIES.ABMS_PROVINCE_SP")
msg("Province polygons: %d", nrow(prov))

# --- Terrain ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Landscape relief. AWS terrain tiles via elevatr, zoom 9, roughly 300 m in
# these latitudes, which is enough for a hillshade at page scale and small
# enough to keep on an 8 GB machine.
dem_path <- file.path(spatial_dir, "dem-z9.tif")
if (!file.exists(dem_path)) {
  # AWS Terrain Tiles, https://registry.opendata.aws/terrain-tiles/
  dem <- elevatr::get_elev_raster(
    locations = sf::st_as_sf(sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(
      sf::st_buffer(basin, 5000)))),
    z = 9, clip = "bbox", prj = sf::st_crs(basin)$wkt)
  terra::writeRaster(terra::rast(dem), dem_path, overwrite = TRUE)
}
dem <- terra::rast(dem_path)
msg("DEM: %d by %d cells, %.0f m resolution, elevation %.0f to %.0f m",
    nrow(dem), ncol(dem), terra::res(dem)[1],
    terra::global(dem, "min", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1],
    terra::global(dem, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1])

# --- Write -----------------------------------------------------------------
if (file.exists(gpkg)) file.remove(gpkg)
w <- function(x, layer) sf::st_write(x, gpkg, layer, quiet = TRUE, append = FALSE)
w(basin, "basin"); w(inc, "ignitions"); w(lakes, "lakes"); w(streams, "streams")
w(places, "places"); w(stations, "stations"); w(era5, "era5_grid")
w(prov, "province")
msg("\nWritten %s", gpkg)

# --- Counts the manuscript cites -------------------------------------------
# Written to derived/ and committed, because the prose quotes them and no number
# may be quoted from code that was not saved.
cause <- as.character(inc$FIRE_CAUSE)
cause[is.na(cause) | cause == ""] <- "Unknown"
counts <- data.frame(
  item = c("watershed_group_id", "watershed_group_name", "basin_area_ha",
           "first_year", "last_year", "n_seasons",
           "ignitions_total", sprintf("ignitions_%s", sort(unique(cause))),
           "fire_weather_stations", "era5_land_cells",
           "dem_min_elev_m", "dem_max_elev_m"),
  value = c(GROUP_ID, basin$WATERSHED_GROUP_NAME, round(basin$AREA_HA),
            FIRST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR, LAST_YEAR - FIRST_YEAR + 1,
            nrow(inc), as.integer(table(cause)[sort(unique(cause))]),
            nrow(stations), nrow(era5),
            round(terra::global(dem, "min", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]),
            round(terra::global(dem, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1])),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
write.csv(counts, file.path(derived_dir, "study-area-counts.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# Per-season ignition counts by cause, so the figure's inset series and any
# prose about the record come from one saved file.
season <- data.frame(year = inc$FIRE_YEAR, cause = cause)
tab <- as.data.frame(table(season$year, season$cause))
names(tab) <- c("fire_year", "fire_cause", "n")
tab$fire_year <- as.integer(as.character(tab$fire_year))
write.csv(tab[order(tab$fire_year, tab$fire_cause), ],
          file.path(derived_dir, "ignitions-by-season.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

msg("Written %s and %s", "02.inputs/derived/study-area-counts.csv",
    "02.inputs/derived/ignitions-by-season.csv")

# --- Integrity manifest ----------------------------------------------------
files <- list.files(spatial_dir, full.names = TRUE, pattern = "[.](gpkg|tif)$")
sums <- vapply(files, function(f) as.character(tools::md5sum(f)), "")
writeLines(sprintf("%s  %s", sums, basename(files)),
           file.path(spatial_dir, "MD5SUMS.txt"))
msg("Retrieved %s. No outcome variable computed.", format(Sys.Date()))
}
```

```{python}
#| label: fetch-fire-weather
#| output: false
"""Retrieve the hourly fire weather record for the Okanagan basin stations.

Written 2026-08-15. Source is the BC Wildfire Service weather data mart, a public
directory published by the BC Ministry of Forests at

    https://www.for.gov.bc.ca/ftp/HPR/external/!publish/BCWS_DATA_MART/

The archive is stored two ways and this script reads both. Seasons 1987 to 2023
are one comma-separated file per year, province wide, named
``<year>/<year>_BCWS_WX_OBS.csv``, the largest of which is roughly 210 MB.
Seasons 2024 onward are one file per calendar day, named ``<year>/<date>.csv``.
Nothing here holds a whole provincial year in memory: each response is streamed
and every row whose station code is not one of the basin stations is dropped as
it arrives.

Station selection is not by bounding box. The five stations are the ones the
BC Data Catalogue layer ``WHSE_LAND_AND_NATURAL_RESOURCE.PROT_WEATHER_STATIONS_SP``
places inside Freshwater Atlas watershed group 161, already clipped to the basin
polygon by the study area chunk above and stored in the ``stations`` layer
of ``02.inputs/spatial/study-area.gpkg``. This script reads that layer rather
than repeating the spatial test, so the two cannot disagree.

The columns kept are the raw hourly observations, the operational FWI1987 codes
that BC Wildfire Service itself computed at the time, and the daily
accumulated precipitation. The operational codes are kept for one purpose: they
are an independent check on this project's own FWI1987 implementation, computed
by a different party with different code, and the series computation chunk
reports the agreement.

Output is written uncompressed to ``02.inputs/weather/bcws-okanagan-hourly.csv``,
which is gitignored for size, together with a small retrieval log at
``02.inputs/derived/fire-weather-retrieval-log.csv`` that is committed.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import datetime as dt
import io
import os
import sys
import time

import requests

BASE = "https://www.for.gov.bc.ca/ftp/HPR/external/!publish/BCWS_DATA_MART"

# Columns carried forward from the data mart. The names are the data mart's own.
KEEP = [
    "STATION_CODE",
    "STATION_NAME",
    "DATE_TIME",
    "HOURLY_PRECIPITATION",
    "HOURLY_TEMPERATURE",
    "HOURLY_RELATIVE_HUMIDITY",
    "HOURLY_WIND_SPEED",
    "HOURLY_WIND_DIRECTION",
    "HOURLY_FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE",
    "HOURLY_INITIAL_SPREAD_INDEX",
    "HOURLY_FIRE_WEATHER_INDEX",
    "PRECIPITATION",
    "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE",
    "DUFF_MOISTURE_CODE",
    "DROUGHT_CODE",
    "INITIAL_SPREAD_INDEX",
    "BUILDUP_INDEX",
    "FIRE_WEATHER_INDEX",
]


def basin_station_codes(root: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Station codes inside watershed group 161, read from the study area package."""
    import geopandas as gpd

    gpkg = os.path.join(root, "02.inputs", "spatial", "study-area.gpkg")
    st = gpd.read_file(gpkg, layer="stations")
    return {str(int(c)): str(n) for c, n in zip(st["STATION_CODE"], st["STATION_NAME"])}


def stream_csv(url: str, session: requests.Session, retries: int = 4):
    """Yield dict rows from a remote CSV without holding the file in memory."""
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            with session.get(url, stream=True, timeout=(30, 600)) as r:
                if r.status_code == 404:
                    return
                r.raise_for_status()
                lines = (
                    b.decode("utf-8-sig", errors="replace")
                    for b in r.iter_lines(chunk_size=1 << 20)
                )
                for row in csv.DictReader(lines):
                    yield row
                return
        except Exception as exc:  # network faults are expected over 4 GB of transfer
            if attempt == retries - 1:
                raise
            print(f"    retry {attempt + 1} after {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", flush=True)
            time.sleep(5 * (attempt + 1))


def main() -> None:
    first, last = 1987, 2025
    root = os.path.abspath("..")
    stations = basin_station_codes(root)
    print("Basin stations:", ", ".join(f"{c} {n}" for c, n in sorted(stations.items())), flush=True)

    out_dir = os.path.join(root, "02.inputs", "weather")
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    out_path = os.path.join(out_dir, "bcws-okanagan-hourly.csv")
    log_path = os.path.join(root, "02.inputs", "derived", "fire-weather-retrieval-log.csv")

    session = requests.Session()
    session.headers["User-Agent"] = "forest-fire-index-trends/1.0 (research; contact repository owner)"

    log: list[dict] = []
    kept_total = 0

    with open(out_path, "w", newline="") as fh:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=KEEP, extrasaction="ignore")
        writer.writeheader()

        for year in range(first, last + 1):
            t0 = time.time()
            kept = 0
            seen = 0

            # BCWS Weather Data Mart, https://www.for.gov.bc.ca/ftp/HPR/external/!publish/BCWS_DATA_MART/
            # Seasons 1987 to 2023: one provincial file per year.
            annual = f"{BASE}/{year}/{year}_BCWS_WX_OBS.csv"
            got_annual = False
            for row in stream_csv(annual, session):
                got_annual = True
                seen += 1
                if str(row.get("STATION_CODE", "")).strip().strip('"') in stations:
                    writer.writerow(row)
                    kept += 1

            # Seasons 2024 onward: one file per calendar day.
            if not got_annual:
                day = dt.date(year, 1, 1)
                end = dt.date(year, 12, 31)
                while day <= end:
                    url = f"{BASE}/{year}/{day.isoformat()}.csv"
                    for row in stream_csv(url, session):
                        seen += 1
                        if str(row.get("STATION_CODE", "")).strip().strip('"') in stations:
                            writer.writerow(row)
                            kept += 1
                    day += dt.timedelta(days=1)

            kept_total += kept
            elapsed = round(time.time() - t0, 1)
            layout = "annual" if got_annual else "daily"
            print(f"{year}  {layout:6s}  rows seen {seen:>9,}  kept {kept:>7,}  {elapsed:>7.1f}s", flush=True)
            log.append(
                {"year": year, "layout": layout, "rows_seen": seen, "rows_kept": kept, "seconds": elapsed}
            )

    with open(log_path, "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=["year", "layout", "rows_seen", "rows_kept", "seconds"])
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(log)

    print(f"\nWrote {kept_total:,} hourly observations to {out_path}", flush=True)
    print(f"Retrieval log at {log_path}", flush=True)


if not os.path.exists(os.path.join("..", "02.inputs", "weather", "bcws-okanagan-hourly.csv")):
    main()
```

```{python}
#| label: fwi1987-system
#| output: false
"""The 1987 Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System, daily, from the 13:00 observation.

Written 2026-08-15. This is FWI1987 as specified by Van Wagner (1987), Forestry
Technical Report 35, whose equations are the FORTRAN listing of Van Wagner and
Pickett (1985), Forestry Technical Report 33. The two changes FWI2025 makes to
the fire behaviour outputs are deliberately NOT applied here: the Initial Spread
Index uses the original wind function, not the Fire Behaviour Prediction System
limiter, because the point of this module is to reproduce the legacy system that
every published Canadian fire danger trend rests on.

Day length factors are the standard Canadian tables. The Duff Moisture Code
factors Le are Van Wagner's table for 46 degrees north and the Drought Code
factors Lf are his table for the same latitude. Canadian operational practice
applies these tables across the country rather than interpolating by latitude,
and BC Wildfire Service does so at the stations used here, so the same tables are
used rather than a latitude adjustment that the comparison series would not share.

Nothing in this module is original. It exists so that FWI1987 and FWI2025 are
computed inside one process from one weather record, and it is checked twice:
against the CRAN package cffdrs, an independent published implementation, and
against the FWI1987 codes BC Wildfire Service itself computed operationally at
these stations at the time. Both checks are run by
the next two chunks and their results are reported in the Results rather than
asserted here.

References
    Van Wagner, C.E. 1987. Development and structure of the Canadian Forest Fire
        Weather Index System. Forestry Technical Report 35. Canadian Forestry
        Service, Ottawa.
    Van Wagner, C.E.; Pickett, T.L. 1985. Equations and FORTRAN program for the
        Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System. Forestry Technical Report 33.
        Canadian Forestry Service, Ottawa.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Van Wagner (1987) Table 3.1: effective day length for the DMC, 46 degrees north.
DAY_LENGTH_DMC = [6.5, 7.5, 9.0, 12.8, 13.9, 13.9, 12.4, 10.9, 9.4, 8.0, 7.0, 6.0]

# Van Wagner (1987) Table 4.1: day length adjustment for the DC, 46 degrees north.
DAY_LENGTH_DC = [-1.6, -1.6, -1.6, 0.9, 3.8, 5.8, 6.4, 5.0, 2.4, 0.4, -1.6, -1.6]

# The coefficient of the FFMC to moisture content transform. Van Wagner (1987,
# equations 2a and 2b, p. 4) and the 1985 FORTRAN listing (statements 110 and
# 150, p. 14) both print 147.2. The value used here is 59.5 * 250 / 101 =
# 147.27722772, which gives a moisture content of exactly 250 per cent at a
# code of zero. The cffdrs package 1.9.2 (FFMC_COEFFICIENT) and the FWI2025
# reference implementation (C_FFMC = 14875 / 101) both use it, and a rounded
# constant would put a difference of its own into the version comparison.
FFMC_COEFFICIENT = 147.2772277227723

# Startup values, Van Wagner (1987) section 6, and the defaults the NG-CFFDRS
# reference implementation uses, so the three series start from one point.
FFMC_START = 85.0
DMC_START = 6.0
DC_START = 15.0


def ffmc(temp: float, rh: float, ws: float, prec: float, ffmc_prev: float) -> float:
    """Fine Fuel Moisture Code. Van Wagner (1987) equations 1 to 10."""
    mo = FFMC_COEFFICIENT * (101.0 - ffmc_prev) / (59.5 + ffmc_prev)  # eq 1

    if prec > 0.5:                                                  # eq 2, 3a, 3b
        rf = prec - 0.5
        # Both the test and the second term take the moisture content before the
        # rain is applied, not after it. Van Wagner writes mo on the right hand
        # side of 3b throughout.
        wetting = 42.5 * rf * math.exp(-100.0 / (251.0 - mo)) * (1.0 - math.exp(-6.93 / rf))
        if mo > 150.0:
            wetting += 0.0015 * (mo - 150.0) ** 2 * math.sqrt(rf)
        mo = min(mo + wetting, 250.0)

    ed = (                                                          # eq 4
        0.942 * rh ** 0.679
        + 11.0 * math.exp((rh - 100.0) / 10.0)
        + 0.18 * (21.1 - temp) * (1.0 - math.exp(-0.115 * rh))
    )

    if mo > ed:
        ko = 0.424 * (1.0 - (rh / 100.0) ** 1.7) + 0.0694 * math.sqrt(ws) * (
            1.0 - (rh / 100.0) ** 8
        )                                                           # eq 6a
        kd = ko * 0.581 * math.exp(0.0365 * temp)                    # eq 6b
        m = ed + (mo - ed) * 10.0 ** (-kd)                           # eq 8
    else:
        ew = (                                                       # eq 5
            0.618 * rh ** 0.753
            + 10.0 * math.exp((rh - 100.0) / 10.0)
            + 0.18 * (21.1 - temp) * (1.0 - math.exp(-0.115 * rh))
        )
        if mo < ew:
            kl = 0.424 * (1.0 - ((100.0 - rh) / 100.0) ** 1.7) + 0.0694 * math.sqrt(
                ws
            ) * (1.0 - ((100.0 - rh) / 100.0) ** 8)                  # eq 7a
            kw = kl * 0.581 * math.exp(0.0365 * temp)                # eq 7b
            m = ew - (ew - mo) * 10.0 ** (-kw)                       # eq 9
        else:
            m = mo

    return max(0.0, min(101.0, 59.5 * (250.0 - m) / (FFMC_COEFFICIENT + m)))  # eq 10


def dmc(temp: float, rh: float, prec: float, dmc_prev: float, month: int) -> float:
    """Duff Moisture Code. Van Wagner (1987) equations 11 to 17."""
    p = dmc_prev

    if prec > 1.5:                                                   # eq 11
        re = 0.92 * prec - 1.27
        # eq 12, in the FORTRAN listing's form, 280 / exp(0.023 P), rather than
        # the paper's 20 + exp((244.72 - P) / 43.43). The two agree to about one
        # part in four thousand and the listing is what the published code runs.
        mo = 20.0 + 280.0 / math.exp(0.023 * p)                       # eq 12
        if p <= 33.0:                                                # eq 13a
            b = 100.0 / (0.5 + 0.3 * p)
        elif p <= 65.0:                                              # eq 13b
            b = 14.0 - 1.3 * math.log(p)
        else:                                                        # eq 13c
            b = 6.2 * math.log(p) - 17.2
        mr = mo + 1000.0 * re / (48.77 + b * re)                      # eq 14
        # eq 15, again in the listing's form: 43.43 (5.6348 - ln(Mr - 20)) rather
        # than the paper's 244.72 - 43.43 ln(Mr - 20). 43.43 x 5.6348 = 244.7194.
        p = max(0.0, 43.43 * (5.6348 - math.log(mr - 20.0)))          # eq 15

    if temp > -1.1:                                                   # eq 16
        k = 1.894 * (temp + 1.1) * (100.0 - rh) * DAY_LENGTH_DMC[month - 1] * 1e-6
    else:
        k = 0.0

    return max(0.0, p + 100.0 * k)                                    # eq 17


def dc(temp: float, prec: float, dc_prev: float, month: int) -> float:
    """Drought Code. Van Wagner (1987) equations 18 to 23."""
    d = dc_prev

    if prec > 2.8:                                                    # eq 18
        rd = 0.83 * prec - 1.27
        qo = 800.0 * math.exp(-d / 400.0)                              # eq 19
        qr = qo + 3.937 * rd                                           # eq 20
        d = max(0.0, 400.0 * math.log(800.0 / qr))                     # eq 21

    v = 0.36 * (max(temp, -2.8) + 2.8) + DAY_LENGTH_DC[month - 1]      # eq 22
    v = max(0.0, v)

    return max(0.0, d + 0.5 * v)                                       # eq 23


def isi(ws: float, ffmc_val: float) -> float:
    """Initial Spread Index, the original wind function. Van Wagner (1987) eq 24 to 26.

    FWI2025 replaces the wind function here with the Fire Behaviour Prediction
    System form, which limits the effect of winds above 40 km/h. That change is
    not applied in this module by design.
    """
    m = FFMC_COEFFICIENT * (101.0 - ffmc_val) / (59.5 + ffmc_val)      # eq 1
    fw = math.exp(0.05039 * ws)                                        # eq 24
    ff = 91.9 * math.exp(-0.1386 * m) * (1.0 + m ** 5.31 / 4.93e7)     # eq 25
    return 0.208 * fw * ff                                             # eq 26


def bui(dmc_val: float, dc_val: float) -> float:
    """Buildup Index. Van Wagner (1987) equations 27a and 27b."""
    if dmc_val == 0.0 and dc_val == 0.0:
        return 0.0
    if dmc_val <= 0.4 * dc_val:                                        # eq 27a
        u = 0.8 * dmc_val * dc_val / (dmc_val + 0.4 * dc_val)
    else:                                                              # eq 27b
        u = dmc_val - (1.0 - 0.8 * dc_val / (dmc_val + 0.4 * dc_val)) * (
            0.92 + (0.0114 * dmc_val) ** 1.7
        )
    return max(0.0, u)


def fwi(isi_val: float, bui_val: float) -> float:
    """Fire Weather Index. Van Wagner (1987) equations 28 to 31."""
    if bui_val <= 80.0:                                                # eq 28a
        fd = 0.626 * bui_val ** 0.809 + 2.0
    else:                                                              # eq 28b
        fd = 1000.0 / (25.0 + 108.64 * math.exp(-0.023 * bui_val))
    b = 0.1 * isi_val * fd                                             # eq 29
    if b > 1.0:                                                        # eq 30
        return math.exp(2.72 * (0.434 * math.log(b)) ** 0.647)
    return b                                                           # eq 31


def dsr(fwi_val: float) -> float:
    """Daily Severity Rating. Van Wagner (1987) equation 32."""
    return 0.0272 * fwi_val ** 1.77


def fwi1987_run(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    ffmc_old: float = FFMC_START,
    dmc_old: float = DMC_START,
    dc_old: float = DC_START,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Run FWI1987 over one station-season of daily 13:00 observations.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df
        Daily weather with columns ``yr``, ``mon``, ``day``, ``temp``, ``rh``,
        ``ws``, ``prec``, in chronological order, one row per day, no gaps.
        Temperature in degrees Celsius, relative humidity in per cent, wind speed
        in kilometres per hour at 10 m, precipitation the 24 hour total in
        millimetres ending at the observation.
    ffmc_old, dmc_old, dc_old
        Startup values carried into the first day.

    Returns
    -------
    The input frame with ``ffmc``, ``dmc``, ``dc``, ``isi``, ``bui``, ``fwi`` and
    ``dsr`` appended.
    """
    out = {k: np.empty(len(df)) for k in ("ffmc", "dmc", "dc", "isi", "bui", "fwi", "dsr")}
    f, p, d = ffmc_old, dmc_old, dc_old

    for i, row in enumerate(df.itertuples(index=False)):
        t, h, w, r, mon = row.temp, row.rh, row.ws, row.prec, int(row.mon)
        # Van Wagner's equations are undefined outside these ranges and the
        # operational convention is to clamp rather than to drop the day.
        h = min(max(h, 0.0), 100.0)
        w = max(w, 0.0)
        r = max(r, 0.0)

        f = ffmc(t, h, w, r, f)
        p = dmc(t, h, r, p, mon)
        d = dc(t, r, d, mon)
        i_ = isi(w, f)
        u = bui(p, d)
        s = fwi(i_, u)

        out["ffmc"][i], out["dmc"][i], out["dc"][i] = f, p, d
        out["isi"][i], out["bui"][i], out["fwi"][i] = i_, u, s
        out["dsr"][i] = dsr(s)

    return df.assign(**out)
```

```{python}
#| label: validate-fwi1987
#| output: false
"""Check this project's FWI1987 module against an independent implementation.

Written 2026-08-15. The FWI1987 chunk above is code written for this study, so
no number it produces is reportable until something else produces the same
number. This script runs the first of two checks: the CRAN package ``cffdrs``,
the implementation published with Wang et al. (2017) and maintained by the
Canadian Forest Service, run over the same input through R.

The test input is the Petawawa Research Forest 2007 daily weather that ships
with the NG-CFFDRS repository, used here only because it is a public file with a
known provenance that both implementations can read. The second check, against
the FWI1987 codes BC Wildfire Service computed operationally at the Okanagan
stations, is run inside the series computation chunk where those codes are
already in hand.

Writes ``02.inputs/derived/fwi1987-validation.csv``, which is committed.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = os.path.abspath("..")
HERE = os.path.join(ROOT, "05.scripts")

R_BIN = "/usr/local/bin/R"

R_SCRIPT = r"""
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(cffdrs))
inp <- read.csv("{inp}")
inp$long <- -abs(inp$long)
# lat.adjust = FALSE holds the day length tables at Van Wagner's 46 degrees north
# values, which is what the Python module uses and what Canadian operational
# practice applies across the country.
out <- fwi(inp, init = c(ffmc = 85, dmc = 6, dc = 15, lat = inp$lat[1]),
           lat.adjust = FALSE)
write.csv(out[, c("FFMC", "DMC", "DC", "ISI", "BUI", "FWI", "DSR")],
          "{out}", row.names = FALSE)
"""


def main() -> None:
    # NG-CFFDRS reference implementation test record, https://github.com/nrcan-cfs-fire/cffdrs-ng
    src = os.path.join(HERE, "vendor", "cffdrs-ng", "PRF2007_daily_wx.csv")
    daily = pd.read_csv(src)

    mine = fwi1987_run(daily.copy())

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        inp = os.path.join(tmp, "in.csv")
        outp = os.path.join(tmp, "out.csv")
        daily.to_csv(inp, index=False)
        script = os.path.join(tmp, "run.R")
        with open(script, "w") as fh:
            fh.write(R_SCRIPT.format(inp=inp, out=outp))
        res = subprocess.run(
            [R_BIN, "--vanilla", "--quiet", "-f", script],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
        )
        if not os.path.exists(outp):
            sys.exit(f"cffdrs run failed:\n{res.stdout}\n{res.stderr}")
        theirs = pd.read_csv(outp)

    rows = []
    for a, b in [("ffmc", "FFMC"), ("dmc", "DMC"), ("dc", "DC"),
                 ("isi", "ISI"), ("bui", "BUI"), ("fwi", "FWI"), ("dsr", "DSR")]:
        x, y = mine[a].to_numpy(float), theirs[b].to_numpy(float)
        rows.append(
            {
                "component": b,
                "n": len(x),
                "max_abs_diff": float(np.nanmax(np.abs(x - y))),
                "mean_abs_diff": float(np.nanmean(np.abs(x - y))),
                "max_value": float(np.nanmax(y)),
            }
        )

    res = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    dest = os.path.join(ROOT, "02.inputs", "derived", "fwi1987-validation.csv")
    res.to_csv(dest, index=False)
    print(res.to_string(index=False))
    print(f"\nWrote {dest}")


if not os.path.exists(os.path.join("..", "02.inputs", "derived", "fwi1987-validation.csv")):
    main()
```

```{python}
#| label: compute-fwi-series
#| output: false
"""Compute the three fire danger series from one Okanagan weather record.

Written 2026-08-15. The design question is that FWI1987 and FWI2025 differ in two
respects at once, the version of the system and the resolution of the weather
driving it, so a two way comparison could not attribute a difference to either.
Three series are computed from a single hourly weather record so that each
contrast moves one thing:

    S1  FWI1987, driven by the daily 13:00 observation.
    S2  FWI2025, driven by the same daily 13:00 observation, pathway C.
    S3  FWI2025, driven by the observed hourly weather, pathway A.

S1 against S2 isolates the version change at fixed input. S2 against S3 isolates
the input resolution change at fixed version. S1 against S3 is the operational
contrast an agency faces and is the sum of the other two.

Weather record
    BC Wildfire Service hourly observations at the five fire weather stations
    inside Freshwater Atlas watershed group 161, retrieved by
    the retrieval chunk above. Timestamps are Pacific Standard Time
    year round, which this script does not assume but verifies: the daily
    FWI1987 codes that BC Wildfire Service computed operationally appear in the
    record at hour 12 and at no other hour, and the standard fire weather
    observation is 13:00 Local Daylight Time, so hour 12 is 13:00 LDT and the
    stamp is Local Standard Time, UTC-8.

Season window
    A fixed calendar window, not a weather derived one. The Canadian rule in
    GLC-X-42 section C-2.3, three days above 12 degrees Celsius where snow cover
    cannot be observed, was implemented first and then abandoned, because these
    stations do not report through the winter and the rule fired on whatever day
    a station was switched on. It produced a "season" of three days at Brenda
    Mines in 1991 and 244 days at Fintry in 1999, and those numbers describe
    field operations rather than climate.

    The window is therefore 1 May to 30 September, 153 days, with the calculation
    spun up from 1 April so that thirty days of weather precede the first reported
    day. One consequence is stated rather than repaired: fire season length cannot
    be estimated from a network whose stations are switched on and off for
    operational reasons, so it is not among the metrics, and the seasonal metrics
    that remain are counts and sums over a window of fixed length.

Startup and overwintering
    Each station season starts from FFMC 85, DMC 6, DC 15, the values Van Wagner
    (1987) gives and the NG-CFFDRS reference implementation defaults to. The
    Drought Code is not overwintered. These stations do not report through the
    winter, so an overwintering calculation would have no weather to run on. The
    same startup is used for all three series, so it cannot bias a contrast
    between them.

Daily summary of the hourly series
    FWI1987 produces one value per day. FWI2025 produces one per hour, and
    GLC-X-42 section 3.1.1 says the daily interpretation may be taken either at a
    user selected hour or at the modelled peak. This script writes both. The
    primary daily value is taken at 16:00 LST, which is 17:00 Local Daylight Time,
    the conventional peak burn hour and, in this record, the modal hour of daily
    maximum temperature. The daily maximum over all 24 hours is written alongside
    it as ``*_max``, and is a sensitivity rather than the primary, because the
    maximum of 24 draws exceeds a single daily value for reasons that have
    nothing to do with the version change.

Gaps
    The reference implementation requires a gap free hourly stream. Runs of
    missing temperature, humidity or wind up to 24 hours are filled by linear
    interpolation; missing precipitation is filled with zero, since rain cannot be
    invented. A station season is kept only when at least 95 per cent of the hours
    from 1 April to 30 September were observed and no single gap exceeded 24
    hours. Every drop is recorded in the coverage table rather than being silently
    absorbed.

    Filling a gap with no rain makes a missing wet spell look dry and pushes fire
    danger up. The direction matters and is stated here: coverage is worse in the
    early record than the late, so this bias, where it acts at all, inflates
    danger early and therefore works against an increasing trend rather than for
    one. It is identical across S1, S2 and S3 by construction, since all three run
    on the same filled record, so it cannot move a contrast between versions.

Outputs, all written to ``02.inputs/derived``:
    ``fwi-series-daily.csv``          one row per station-day, the three series.
    ``fwi-station-season-coverage.csv``  what was kept, what was dropped, and why.
    ``fwi1987-operational-check.csv``    S1 against BC Wildfire Service's own codes.

Each station season is independent, because the moisture codes are carried forward
within a season and reset at its start, so nothing crosses the boundary. The work
could be split across processes; the hourly loop inside the reference
implementation is pure Python and is the whole cost of this chunk.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sys
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ROOT = os.path.abspath("..")
HERE = os.path.join(ROOT, "05.scripts")
# NG-CFFDRS reference implementation, https://github.com/nrcan-cfs-fire/cffdrs-ng,
# vendored at the commit recorded in 05.scripts/vendor/cffdrs-ng/COMMIT.txt.
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(HERE, "vendor", "cffdrs-ng"))
from make_minmax import daily_to_minmax  # noqa: E402
from make_hourly import minmax_to_hourly  # noqa: E402
from NG_FWI import hFWI  # noqa: E402
from daily_summaries import generate_daily_summaries  # noqa: E402

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)

TIMEZONE = -8.0          # Pacific Standard Time, verified below, not assumed
NOON_HOUR = 12           # 13:00 Local Daylight Time, the standard observation
PEAK_HOUR = 16           # 17:00 Local Daylight Time, the conventional peak burn hour

SPINUP_MONTH_DAY = (4, 1)   # calculation starts here, 30 days before reporting
WINDOW_START = (5, 1)       # metrics are reported from here
WINDOW_END = (9, 30)        # to here, 153 days

MAX_GAP_HOURS = 24
MIN_OBSERVED_FRACTION = 0.95

COMPONENTS = ["ffmc", "dmc", "dc", "isi", "bui", "fwi", "dsr"]

# The station season whose hourly output is written out whole for the mechanism
# figure. Penticton RS, station 328, is the longest record in the basin, and 2003
# is the season of the Okanagan Mountain Park fire.
EXAMPLE_SEASON = ("328", 2003)


def load_hourly(path: str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read the retrieved record and put it into the reference implementation's names."""
    path = path or os.path.join(ROOT, "02.inputs", "weather", "bcws-okanagan-hourly.csv")
    d = pd.read_csv(path, low_memory=False)
    d["DATE_TIME"] = d["DATE_TIME"].astype(str).str.strip().str.strip('"')
    d = d[d["DATE_TIME"].str.len() == 10].copy()

    d["yr"] = d["DATE_TIME"].str[0:4].astype(int)
    d["mon"] = d["DATE_TIME"].str[4:6].astype(int)
    d["day"] = d["DATE_TIME"].str[6:8].astype(int)
    d["hr"] = d["DATE_TIME"].str[8:10].astype(int)

    for src, dst in [
        ("HOURLY_TEMPERATURE", "temp"),
        ("HOURLY_RELATIVE_HUMIDITY", "rh"),
        ("HOURLY_WIND_SPEED", "ws"),
        ("HOURLY_PRECIPITATION", "prec"),
    ]:
        d[dst] = pd.to_numeric(d[src], errors="coerce")

    d["id"] = d["STATION_CODE"].astype(str).str.strip().str.strip('"')
    d["timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(
        dict(year=d.yr, month=d.mon, day=d.day, hour=d.hr), errors="coerce"
    )
    d = d[d["timestamp"].notna()].copy()
    return d.sort_values(["id", "timestamp"]).reset_index(drop=True)


def verify_timezone(d: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """Confirm that the operational daily codes sit at hour 12 and nowhere else."""
    by_hour = d.groupby("hr")["FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"].apply(lambda s: s.notna().sum())
    at_noon = int(by_hour.get(NOON_HOUR, 0))
    elsewhere = int(by_hour.drop(index=NOON_HOUR, errors="ignore").sum())
    if at_noon == 0 or elsewhere > 0:
        sys.exit(
            "Daily codes are not stamped exclusively at hour 12; the timezone "
            f"assumption fails. At hour 12: {at_noon}. At other hours: {elsewhere}."
        )
    summer = d[(d.mon.isin([6, 7, 8])) & d.temp.notna()].copy()
    peak = summer.loc[summer.groupby(["id", "yr", "mon", "day"])["temp"].idxmax(), "hr"]
    return {
        "daily_codes_at_hour_12": at_noon,
        "daily_codes_at_other_hours": elsewhere,
        "modal_hour_of_max_temp_summer": int(peak.mode().iloc[0]),
    }


def quality_control(d: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Void observations outside the physically possible range for this basin."""
    d.loc[(d.temp < -50) | (d.temp > 50), "temp"] = np.nan
    d.loc[(d.rh < 0) | (d.rh > 100), "rh"] = np.nan
    d.loc[(d.ws < 0) | (d.ws > 200), "ws"] = np.nan
    d.loc[(d.prec < 0) | (d.prec > 200), "prec"] = np.nan
    return d


def window_bounds(year: int) -> tuple[pd.Timestamp, pd.Timestamp, pd.Timestamp]:
    """Spin-up start, reporting start and reporting end for one season."""
    spin = pd.Timestamp(year, *SPINUP_MONTH_DAY)
    start = pd.Timestamp(year, *WINDOW_START)
    end = pd.Timestamp(year, *WINDOW_END)
    return spin, start, end


def fill_gaps(h: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, int, int]:
    """Reindex to a complete hourly stream and fill short gaps.

    Returns the filled frame, the number of hours filled, and the longest run of
    consecutive filled hours.
    """
    full = pd.date_range(h["timestamp"].min(), h["timestamp"].max(), freq="h")
    h = h.set_index("timestamp").reindex(full)
    h.index.name = "timestamp"

    missing = h[["temp", "rh", "ws"]].isna().any(axis=1)
    n_filled = int(missing.sum())
    longest = 0
    run = 0
    for flag in missing.to_numpy():
        run = run + 1 if flag else 0
        longest = max(longest, run)

    for c in ("temp", "rh", "ws"):
        h[c] = h[c].interpolate(limit_direction="both")
    h["prec"] = h["prec"].fillna(0.0)

    h = h.reset_index()
    h["yr"] = h.timestamp.dt.year
    h["mon"] = h.timestamp.dt.month
    h["day"] = h.timestamp.dt.day
    h["hr"] = h.timestamp.dt.hour
    return h, n_filled, longest


def noon_daily(h: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The daily 13:00 LDT observation with the preceding 24 hours of rain.

    The 24 hour total is accumulated from the hourly record over the window that
    ends at the observation, which is what the FWI1987 input is defined to be,
    rather than the calendar day total.
    """
    h = h.sort_values("timestamp").reset_index(drop=True)
    # Rolling 24 hour rainfall ending at each hour, inclusive of that hour.
    h = h.set_index("timestamp")
    h["prec24"] = h["prec"].rolling("24h").sum()
    h = h.reset_index()

    noon = h[h.hr == NOON_HOUR].copy()
    noon["prec"] = noon["prec24"]
    noon["date"] = noon["timestamp"].dt.normalize()
    return noon[["id", "lat", "long", "timezone", "yr", "mon", "day", "date",
                 "temp", "rh", "ws", "prec"]].reset_index(drop=True)


def summarise_hourly(res: pd.DataFrame, tag: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Reduce an hourly FWI2025 run to one row per day, three ways.

    The primary daily value is taken at a fixed hour, so that it is one draw and
    not the maximum of 24. The daily maximum is carried alongside as a
    sensitivity. The specification's own daily summary is carried too, because it
    reports two quantities FWI1987 cannot produce at all: the hour at which peak
    burning conditions occur, and the number of hours the burning window stays
    open. Those are a capability difference rather than a level difference and
    they are reported as such.
    """
    res = res.copy()
    res["date"] = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=res.yr, month=res.mon, day=res.day))

    at_peak = res[res.hr == PEAK_HOUR].set_index("date")[COMPONENTS]
    at_peak.columns = [f"{tag}_{c}" for c in COMPONENTS]

    daily_max = res.groupby("date")[COMPONENTS].max()
    daily_max.columns = [f"{tag}_{c}_max" for c in COMPONENTS]

    out = at_peak.join(daily_max, how="outer")

    try:
        rep = generate_daily_summaries(res, silent=True)
        rep["date"] = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=rep.yr, month=rep.mon, day=rep.day))
        rep = rep.set_index("date")[["peak_hr", "duration", "isi_smooth"]]
        rep.columns = [f"{tag}_{c}" for c in rep.columns]
        out = out.join(rep, how="left")
    except Exception as exc:  # the summary is supplementary, not load bearing
        print(f"    daily summaries unavailable for {tag}: {exc}", flush=True)

    return out


def _run_station_season(task):
    """Compute the three series for one station season.

    Returns a tuple of (coverage record, daily output or None, operational check
    rows, example frame or None, progress message). Written as a free function
    taking one argument so that it can be handed to a process pool: the season is
    the natural unit of parallelism, because the moisture codes are carried
    forward within a season and reset at its start, so nothing crosses the
    boundary.
    """
    sid, yr, (lat, lon, name, elev), g = task

    if g is None:
        return ({
            "station_code": sid, "station_name": name, "year": int(yr),
            "elevation_m": elev, "expected_hours": np.nan, "observed_hours": 0,
            "observed_fraction": 0.0, "filled_hours": np.nan,
            "longest_gap_h": np.nan, "status": "station not reporting",
        }, None, [], None, None)

    g = g.sort_values("timestamp")
    spin, wstart, wend = window_bounds(int(yr))
    expected = int((wend + pd.Timedelta(days=1) - spin).total_seconds() // 3600)

    window = g[(g.timestamp >= spin) & (g.timestamp < wend + pd.Timedelta(days=1))].copy()
    # One row per hour: the data mart occasionally repeats a timestamp.
    window = window.drop_duplicates(subset="timestamp", keep="first")
    observed = int(window[["temp", "rh", "ws"]].notna().all(axis=1).sum())

    rec = {
        "station_code": sid,
        "station_name": name,
        "year": int(yr),
        "elevation_m": elev,
        "expected_hours": expected,
        "observed_hours": observed,
        "observed_fraction": round(observed / expected, 4),
    }

    if observed == 0:
        rec.update(status="no data in window", filled_hours=np.nan, longest_gap_h=np.nan)
        return (rec, None, [], None, None)

    # Reindex over the whole spin-up-to-window span, not merely over the hours the
    # station happened to report, so that a station switched on in July counts the
    # preceding months as missing rather than as absent.
    window = window.set_index("timestamp").reindex(
        pd.date_range(spin, wend + pd.Timedelta(hours=23), freq="h")
    ).reset_index(names="timestamp")

    h, n_filled, longest = fill_gaps(window[["timestamp", "temp", "rh", "ws", "prec"]])
    h["id"], h["lat"], h["long"], h["timezone"] = sid, lat, lon, TIMEZONE

    rec.update(filled_hours=n_filled, longest_gap_h=longest)
    if rec["observed_fraction"] < MIN_OBSERVED_FRACTION or longest > MAX_GAP_HOURS:
        rec["status"] = "dropped, coverage"
        return (rec, None, [], None, None)
    rec["status"] = "kept"

    daily = noon_daily(h)
    if len(daily) < 150:
        rec["status"] = "dropped, short season"
        return (rec, None, [], None, None)

    # S1: FWI1987 on the daily 13:00 observation.
    s1 = fwi1987_run(daily.copy())
    s1 = s1.set_index("date")[COMPONENTS]
    s1.columns = [f"s1_{c}" for c in COMPONENTS]

    # S2: FWI2025 pathway C, the same daily observation estimated to hourly.
    d13 = daily[["id", "lat", "long", "timezone", "yr", "mon", "day",
                 "temp", "rh", "ws", "prec"]].copy()
    mm = daily_to_minmax(d13, silent=True)
    hourly_c = minmax_to_hourly(mm, silent=True)
    run_c = hFWI(hourly_c, silent=True)
    s2 = summarise_hourly(run_c, "s2")

    # S3: FWI2025 pathway A, the observed hourly weather.
    hourly_a = h[["id", "lat", "long", "timezone", "yr", "mon", "day", "hr",
                  "temp", "rh", "ws", "prec"]].copy()
    run_a = hFWI(hourly_a, silent=True)
    s3 = summarise_hourly(run_a, "s3")

    # One station season of the hourly runs is kept whole, so that the mechanism
    # figure in the manuscript draws real hourly output rather than an illustration.
    example = None
    if (sid, int(yr)) == EXAMPLE_SEASON:
        ex = run_a[["yr", "mon", "day", "hr", "temp", "rh", "ws", "prec",
                    "ffmc", "isi", "fwi", "sunrise", "sunset"]].copy()
        ex.columns = [c if c in ("yr", "mon", "day", "hr") else f"s3_{c}"
                      for c in ex.columns]
        exc = run_c[["yr", "mon", "day", "hr", "temp", "rh", "ws", "prec",
                     "ffmc", "isi", "fwi"]].copy()
        exc.columns = [c if c in ("yr", "mon", "day", "hr") else f"s2_{c}"
                       for c in exc.columns]
        example = ex.merge(exc, on=["yr", "mon", "day", "hr"], how="inner")

    out = s1.join(s2, how="left").join(s3, how="left")
    # April is spin-up only. The codes it produces are still carrying the startup
    # values and are not reported.
    out = out[(out.index >= wstart) & (out.index <= wend)]
    out.insert(0, "station_code", sid)
    out.insert(1, "station_name", name)
    out.insert(2, "year", int(yr))
    out = out.reset_index()

    # Independent check: BC Wildfire Service's own operational FWI1987 codes.
    checks = []
    ops = g[g.hr == NOON_HOUR][
        ["timestamp", "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE", "DUFF_MOISTURE_CODE",
         "DROUGHT_CODE", "INITIAL_SPREAD_INDEX", "BUILDUP_INDEX", "FIRE_WEATHER_INDEX"]
    ].copy()
    ops["date"] = ops["timestamp"].dt.normalize()
    merged = ops.set_index("date").join(s1, how="inner")
    for a, b in [("FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE", "s1_ffmc"),
                 ("DUFF_MOISTURE_CODE", "s1_dmc"),
                 ("DROUGHT_CODE", "s1_dc"),
                 ("INITIAL_SPREAD_INDEX", "s1_isi"),
                 ("BUILDUP_INDEX", "s1_bui"),
                 ("FIRE_WEATHER_INDEX", "s1_fwi")]:
        x = pd.to_numeric(merged[a], errors="coerce")
        y = merged[b]
        ok = x.notna() & y.notna()
        if ok.sum() >= 20:
            checks.append({
                "station_code": sid, "year": int(yr), "component": a,
                "n": int(ok.sum()),
                "pearson_r": float(np.corrcoef(x[ok], y[ok])[0, 1]),
                "mean_bias": float((y[ok] - x[ok]).mean()),
                "rmse": float(np.sqrt(((y[ok] - x[ok]) ** 2).mean())),
            })

    msg = f"  {name:14s} {yr}  days {len(daily):>3}  filled {n_filled:>3}"
    return (rec, out, checks, example, msg)


def main() -> None:
    # One process. The pool below needs a module to spawn from, which a chunk
    # is not, so the station seasons run in sequence.
    jobs = 1

    d = load_hourly()
    tz_check = verify_timezone(d)
    print("Timezone verification:", tz_check, flush=True)

    d = quality_control(d)

    stations = pd.read_csv(
        os.path.join(ROOT, "02.inputs", "derived", "station-metadata.csv")
    ) if os.path.exists(
        os.path.join(ROOT, "02.inputs", "derived", "station-metadata.csv")
    ) else None
    if stations is None:
        import geopandas as gpd

        st = gpd.read_file(
            os.path.join(ROOT, "02.inputs", "spatial", "study-area.gpkg"), layer="stations"
        )
        stations = st[["STATION_CODE", "STATION_NAME", "LATITUDE", "LONGITUDE", "ELEVATION"]].copy()
        stations["STATION_CODE"] = stations["STATION_CODE"].astype(int).astype(str)
        stations.to_csv(
            os.path.join(ROOT, "02.inputs", "derived", "station-metadata.csv"), index=False
        )
    # The station code is an identifier, not a number. Reading the cached CSV
    # back turns it into an integer and the join against the weather record,
    # whose codes are strings, then silently matches nothing.
    stations["STATION_CODE"] = stations["STATION_CODE"].astype(str).str.strip()
    meta = {
        r.STATION_CODE: (float(r.LATITUDE), float(r.LONGITUDE), r.STATION_NAME, float(r.ELEVATION))
        for r in stations.itertuples()
    }
    if not set(meta) & set(d["id"].unique()):
        sys.exit(f"No station code in the weather record matches the station table: "
                 f"{sorted(meta)} against {sorted(d['id'].unique())}")
```
