@fig-ignitions shows the records season by season, and the fall of both completeness measures after 2000 made the cause split unreadable as an ignition trend. Three response series were therefore modelled, lightning, person-caused and all causes together, because the all-cause series was unaffected by cause coding and so decided any disagreement. Recording of small fires also changed over the record. Among incidents with a recorded size, the share under 0.1 ha was `r min(small$pct_small)` per cent in the `r small$decade[which.min(small$pct_small)]` and `r max(small$pct_small)` per cent in the `r small$decade[which.max(small$pct_small)]`. Every result was therefore reported at three minimum fire sizes, no limit, one hectare and four hectares. A conclusion that survived at only one was reported as not surviving.

## Statistical Analysis

### Trends

Trends were estimated with the Theil-Sen slope [@sen1968slope] and tested with the Mann-Kendall test [@mann1945nonparametric] over the `r n_seasons` kept seasons from `r yr_first` to `r yr_last`. Both were computed on the actual season years, so that a gap was kept as a gap.

Significance was assessed under the variance correction of @hamed1998mmk for serial correlation, without which the test rejected too often on trendless series [@yue2002autocorrelation; @bayazit2007prewhiten]. The correction counted lags in observations rather than years, so across a gap left by the coverage rule it was understated. A marginal q value, the p value after correction for multiple testing, was therefore weaker than it read.

Within each station's twelve metrics in each series, p values were corrected by the false discovery rate procedure of @benjamini1995fdr. @benjamini2001dependency proved that it still controlled that rate under positive regression dependency, the case here. The families, one per station and series, shared one basin's weather, so tests in different families were positively dependent as well as tests within one. The family was set at the station because each trend was a question about one station's record. The confidence interval on a slope was the percentile interval over 2,000 moving-block bootstrap resamples of seasons.

### Slope Differences

The difference between two series' slopes was tested on the differences themselves, following @santer2000trenddiff, by a moving-block bootstrap, because the three series were mutually dependent and serially correlated [@kunsch1989bootstrap; @politis1994stationary]. Each of the 4,000 replicates drew blocks of consecutive seasons with replacement and recomputed both slopes on the same resampled seasons, keeping the pairing between series [@wilks1997resampling]. The difference test drew twice the replicates of the slope interval, because its p value was read from the tail of the resampled distribution and then corrected for false discovery. Blocks were `r paste(sort(unique(vapply(as.integer(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15]), block_length, integer(1)))), collapse = ' or ')` seasons long for station records of `r min(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15])` to `r max(table(kept$station_name))` seasons, the cube root of the record length rounded up [@kunsch1989bootstrap]. They were drawn in order of occurrence, so that a gap fell inside a block. The interval on the difference was the percentile interval. The two-sided p value followed the first guideline of @hall1991guidelines and was corrected for false discovery rate within the twelve metrics of one contrast at one station. The resampled differences were centred on the observed difference, and p was the share of them at least as far from it as the observed difference was from zero.

### Ignition Models

Daily ignition counts were modelled by negative binomial regression with a log link [@lawless1987negbin], in the daily form of @plucinski2014bushfires. The linear predictor contained the series' Fire Weather Index averaged over the `r n_core` core stations that day. It also contained two annual harmonics in day of year after @martell1989seasonal, and season as a factor. The core stations were those present in at least 80 per cent of the kept seasons, and the number of them reporting that day was a further term. The season factor gave each season its own intercept, so the danger coefficient was identified only from day-to-day variation inside a season. Within a season, reporting completeness and cause coding did not change. The lightning model had no strike term, because no public record of strikes covered the seasons. The Canadian Lightning Detection Network "was established in 1998 and consists of over 80 lightning sensors distributed across Canada" [@eccc2016cldn], `r 1998 - yr_first` years after this record began. Environment and Climate Change Canada "does not have a website for historical lightning", and historical data came "by contacting your weather service" [@eccc2018lightningfaq]. Stationarity was tested by an interaction between the danger term and season number. This was the count form of the period by intensity interactions that @granville2022case fitted to industrial fires in Ontario from 1976 to 2019. The season effect followed @magnussen2012bc, whose year-specific British Columbia models showed coefficients varying between years "typically in excess of 100%" [@magnussen2012bc, p. 346].

Predictive skill was compared by the blocked cross-validation that @roberts2017crossvalidation recommended, in the leave-one-year-out form of @magnussen2012bc. Each season was left out in turn and scored by its log likelihood under the model refitted without it, the strictly proper logarithmic score of @gneiting2007scoring. The scores were comparable because the three series were scored on the same days. Because the three were close to transformations of one another, a small difference in held-out likelihood was not read as a difference in predictive power [@eastaugh2012cautionary].

### Detectable Trend

Following @weatherhead1998detection, the minimum detectable trend for each metric over `r n_seasons` seasons was the slope at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 reached 90 per cent power. The power was computed from the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line. The slope was adjusted for the lower efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator. It was then inflated for serial correlation by the factor @weatherhead1998detection derived for first-order autoregressive noise, the square root of (1 + phi) / (1 − phi). Phi was the lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals in season order, bounded between 0 and 0.9.

# Results {#sec-results}

```{r}
#| label: load-results
#| output: false
series_daily <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi-series-daily.csv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
series_daily$date <- as.Date(series_daily$date)
metrics <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "seasonal-metrics.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
thresh_pct <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "threshold-percentiles.csv"),
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "basin-daily.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin$date <- as.Date(basin$date)

# Relative-threshold counts are replaced by the in-base bootstrap estimates of
# Zhang et al. (2005), computed from the same daily series and the same
# 1991 to 2020 base period. Out-of-base seasons are unchanged by construction;
# the check below stops the render if any is not.
corrected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SERIES), function(s)
  inbase_corrected_counts(series_daily, s, probs = c(90, 95),
                          reference = c(1991, 2020))))
for (pp in c(90, 95)) {
  col <- paste0("n_fwi_p", pp)
  cc <- corrected[corrected$prob == pp, c("station_name", "series", "year", "count")]
  key_m <- paste(metrics$station_name, metrics$series, metrics$year)
  key_c <- paste(cc$station_name, cc$series, cc$year)
  new <- cc$count[match(key_m, key_c)]
  out_base <- metrics$year > 2020 & is.finite(metrics[[col]])
  if (any(abs(new[out_base] - metrics[[col]][out_base]) > 1e-9))
    stop("in-base correction changed an out-of-base count for ", col)
  metrics[[paste0(col, "_uncorrected")]] <- metrics[[col]]
  metrics[[col]] <- new
}
corrected_isi <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SERIES), function(s)
  inbase_corrected_counts(series_daily, s, probs = 95,
                          reference = c(1991, 2020), component = "isi")))
cc <- corrected_isi[, c("station_name", "series", "year", "count")]
key_m <- paste(metrics$station_name, metrics$series, metrics$year)
key_c <- paste(cc$station_name, cc$series, cc$year)
new <- cc$count[match(key_m, key_c)]
out_base <- metrics$year > 2020 & is.finite(metrics$n_isi_p95)
if (any(abs(new[out_base] - metrics$n_isi_p95[out_base]) > 1e-9))
  stop("in-base correction changed an out-of-base count for n_isi_p95")
metrics$n_isi_p95_uncorrected <- metrics$n_isi_p95
metrics$n_isi_p95 <- new
```

Results followed the order of the design. Where each absolute threshold fell in each series came first, then the diurnal mechanism that separated the series, then the three questions in turn.

## Threshold Positions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Where each absolute threshold falls in each series' own 1991 to 2020 reference distribution, averaged over stations. A threshold at the same percentile in every series would mean the three systems are interchangeable for counting extremes. The reference median is the median of that component over the same distribution."
tp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(thresh_pct, list(thresh_pct$series, thresh_pct$component,
                         thresh_pct$threshold), drop = TRUE),
  function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Component = toupper(d$component[1]),
    Threshold = d$threshold[1],
    `Percentile of threshold` = round(mean(d$percentile_of_threshold, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days per season above` = NA_real_,
    `Reference median` = round(mean(d$reference_median, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
# Days per season above each absolute threshold, averaged over station-seasons.
days_above <- function(series, component, thr) {
  col <- switch(paste(component, thr),
                "ffmc 91" = "n_ffmc_gt91",
                "fwi 19" = "n_fwi_gt19",
                "fwi 30" = "n_fwi_gt30")
  mean(metrics[[col]][metrics$series == series], na.rm = TRUE)
}
key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(tp), "\\."))
tp$`Days per season above` <- round(mapply(days_above, key[, 1], key[, 2],
                                           as.numeric(key[, 3])), 1)
tp <- tp[order(tp$Component, tp$Threshold, tp$Series), ]
rownames(tp) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tp)
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-prose
#| output: false
ffmc91 <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
fwi19 <- subset(tp, Component == "FWI" & Threshold == 19)
p_s1 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s2 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s3 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s1 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s2 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s3 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
# Spread of the three reference medians, the level comparison the sentence states.
med_spread <- diff(range(ffmc91$`Reference median`))
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-reading
#| output: false
# The comparability claim is about where a value sits, so the reading is stated
# in the two units that matter and neither is rounded away: the percentile spread
# across series, and the difference in days per season an agency would count.
pct_spread <- max(abs(p_s3 - p_s1), abs(p_s2 - p_s1))
day_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
day_gap_pct <- 100 * day_gap / d_s1
# The same migration gap at the two Fire Weather Index thresholds.
fwi30 <- subset(tp, Component == "FWI" & Threshold == 30)
gap_at <- function(d) d$`Days per season above`[grepl("S3", d$Series)] -
  d$`Days per season above`[grepl("S1", d$Series)]
gap19 <- gap_at(fwi19)
gap30 <- gap_at(fwi30)
```

Over the reference period of 1991 to 2020, the statement of @cffdg2025fwi2025 [p. 17] that "an FFMC of 91 in FWI1987 should correspond to an FFMC of approximately 91 in FWI2025" held for the value and not for the count of days above it (@tbl-thresholds). The three reference medians of the Fine Fuel Moisture Code lay within `r sprintf("%.1f", med_spread)` units of each other. A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 fell at the `r p_s1`th percentile of the S1 distribution, the `r p_s2`th of S2 and the `r p_s3`th of S3. The same threshold nonetheless selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` `r if (day_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under S3 than under S1, a difference of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(day_gap_pct))` per cent, because the percentile it occupied moved by `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_spread)` points. Under the migration, the count above a Fire Weather Index of 19 moved by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(gap19))` days per season and above 30 by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(gap30))`. Before the revision, @hanes2021classes [p. 2] had written that "while modifications to the FWI System are being planned to reproduce the general existing range in observed outputs, some differences in the frequency of occurrence of different codes or index values may result".

```{r}
#| label: level-shifts
#| output: false
# The level shift each change produces, per season, on the two absolute-threshold
# counts and on the three level metrics whose equations the 2025 revision
# rewrote. The sign is computed, not asserted, because the two changes do not
# necessarily push the same way. Moved here from the Discussion on 2026-11-05,
# since a shift between series is a result.
lvl <- function(metric, a, b) {
  mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == b], na.rm = TRUE) -
    mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == a], na.rm = TRUE)
}
shift_cols <- c("n_ffmc_gt91", "n_fwi_gt19", "mean_isi", "mean_dmc", "peak_dc")
shift <- data.frame(
  metric = c("Days FFMC > 91", "Days FWI > 19", "Mean ISI", "Mean DMC", "Peak DC"),
  unit = c("days", "days", "ISI units", "DMC units", "DC units"),
  version = sapply(shift_cols, lvl, a = "s1", b = "s2"),
  input = sapply(shift_cols, lvl, a = "s2", b = "s3"),
  migration = sapply(shift_cols, lvl, a = "s1", b = "s3"),
  row.names = NULL
)
# The migration shift as a share of the FWI1987 level of the same metric.
base_s1 <- sapply(shift_cols, function(m) mean(metrics[[m]][metrics$series == "s1"], na.rm = TRUE))
shift$migration_pct <- 100 * shift$migration / base_s1
write.csv(shift, file.path(outputs, "level-shifts.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
# Direction words for the prose, computed so that a sentence cannot assert a
# sign the numbers do not show.
up_down <- function(x, up = "raised", down = "lowered") if (x >= 0) up else down
```

Across the kept station-seasons, the version change at fixed 13:00 input moved the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[1])` days per season. The input resolution change moved it by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[1])`. On the count above a Fire Weather Index of 19, the two changes moved it by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])` days. The version change `r up_down(shift$version[4])` the mean Duff Moisture Code by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$version[4]))` units and `r up_down(shift$version[5])` the peak Drought Code by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$version[5]))` units. The hourly input then moved them by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[4])` and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[5])` units. The mean Initial Spread Index moved by `r sprintf("%+.2f", shift$version[3])` under the version change and by `r sprintf("%+.2f", shift$input[3])` under the input change. Over both changes, the migration netted `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[1])` days at the first threshold and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` at the second. It left the Duff Moisture Code `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$migration_pct[4]))` per cent `r up_down(shift$migration[4], "higher", "lower")` and the Drought Code `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$migration_pct[5]))` per cent `r up_down(shift$migration[5], "higher", "lower")` than under FWI1987.

## Mechanism

```{r}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Ten days of the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code at Penticton RS in August 2003, under FWI2025 driven by the observed hourly weather and under FWI2025 driven by the 13:00 observation alone. Both are the same system on the same days, and the only difference is the weather input the System received. The vertical lines mark 13:00 local daylight time, the hour FWI1987 observes, and 17:00, the hour a daily value conventionally represents."
# One colour per series, shared by every figure that follows.
cols <- c(s1 = "#1B4F72", s2 = "#B7950B", s3 = "#943126")
ex <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "example-season-hourly.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ex$t <- as.POSIXct(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:00:00", ex$yr, ex$mon, ex$day, ex$hr),
                   tz = "UTC")
win <- ex[ex$mon == 8 & ex$day >= 14 & ex$day <= 23, ]

op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 4, 1.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
plot(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, type = "l", col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6,
     ylim = range(c(win$s3_ffmc, win$s2_ffmc), na.rm = TRUE),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", xaxt = "n")
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
axis.POSIXct(1, win$t, format = "%d %b")
# The hour markers are drawn thin and pale on purpose: they locate the two
# sampling hours without competing with the curves, which are the subject.
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 12], col = "grey86", lty = 3, lwd = 0.6)
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 16], col = "grey62", lty = 2, lwd = 0.6)
lines(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6)
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c(unname(SERIES[c("s3", "s2")]),
                  "13:00 LDT, the FWI1987 observation", "17:00 LDT"),
       col = c(cols["s3"], cols["s2"], "grey86", "grey62"),
       lwd = c(1.6, 1.6, 0.8, 0.8), lty = c(1, 1, 3, 2))
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: capability-summary
#| output: false
# The two quantities FWI2025 reports and FWI1987 cannot, the hour of peak burning
# conditions and the hours per day the burning window stays open, as the
# specification's own daily summary computes them, averaged over kept
# station-seasons. Read by the sentences below and by the Conclusions.
cap <- metrics[metrics$series %in% c("s2", "s3") &
                 !is.na(metrics$mean_peak_hr), ]
if (nrow(cap)) {
  ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cap, cap$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Mean peak hour (LST)` = round(mean(d$mean_peak_hr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Mean burning window (h)` = round(mean(d$mean_duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Days per season with window >= 6 h` = round(mean(d$n_duration_ge6, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    # Spread across station-seasons, so that each mean carries its dispersion.
    `SD peak hour (h)` = round(sd(d$mean_peak_hr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `SD burning window (h)` = round(sd(d$mean_duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `SD days with window >= 6 h` = round(sd(d$n_duration_ge6, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
} else {
  stop("seasonal-metrics.csv carries no daily summary columns; re-run build_seasonal_metrics.py")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mechanism-reading
#| output: false
# The two readings the figure supports, computed from the same window it draws.
night <- win$hr %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5)
day <- win$hr %in% c(14, 15, 16, 17)
night_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[night] - win$s2_ffmc[night], na.rm = TRUE)
day_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[day] - win$s2_ffmc[day], na.rm = TRUE)
range_s3 <- mean(tapply(win$s3_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
range_s2 <- mean(tapply(win$s2_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
# The capability summary by series, and a decimal hour written as a clock time.
cap_s2 <- ct[grepl("S2", ct$Series), ]
cap_s3 <- ct[grepl("S3", ct$Series), ]
clock <- function(h) sprintf("%02d:%02d", floor(h), round((h - floor(h)) * 60))
```

At Penticton RS over ten days in August 2003, the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code under S2 differed in shape from the code under S3 (@fig-mechanism). S2 was reconstructed from the 13:00 observation and S3 ran on the observed hourly weather. The reconstructed code moved `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s2)` units between its daily minimum and maximum against `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s3)` for the observed series. The two ran `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` units apart in mid-afternoon and `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(night_gap))` units apart before dawn, so the reconstruction estimated the nights wetter than observed. Two quantities were produced only by FWI2025, the hour of peak burning conditions and the number of hours a day the burning window stayed open. Both came from the daily summaries the report offered "as examples and starting points" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 27]. The hour of peak burning conditions was the hour of the highest smoothed Initial Spread Index. On days whose highest Fine Fuel Moisture Code stayed below 85, the hour of peak burning conditions was set to 17:00 local standard time. The window opened when the smoothed Initial Spread Index first reached a threshold "equal to or greater than five, which corresponds to spreading surface fires" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 28]. It closed when the index last fell below it, and the report judged it "might be useful for understanding the impacts of non-standard conditions" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 28]. Over kept station-seasons, the mean hour of peak burning conditions was `r clock(cap_s2[["Mean peak hour (LST)"]])` under S2 and `r clock(cap_s3[["Mean peak hour (LST)"]])` under S3, in local standard time. The standard deviations across station-seasons were `r round(60 * cap_s2[["SD peak hour (h)"]])` and `r round(60 * cap_s3[["SD peak hour (h)"]])` minutes. The mean burning window was `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s2[["Mean burning window (h)"]])` hours under S2 and `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s3[["Mean burning window (h)"]])` hours under S3, with standard deviations of `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s2[["SD burning window (h)"]])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s3[["SD burning window (h)"]])` hours. Days per season with a window of at least six hours numbered `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s2[["Days per season with window >= 6 h"]])` under S2 and `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s3[["Days per season with window >= 6 h"]])` under S3, with standard deviations of `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s2[["SD days with window >= 6 h"]])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", cap_s3[["SD days with window >= 6 h"]])` days.

## Trends

```{r}
#| label: trend-compute
#| output: false
# The metric family. Each entry is a column of the seasonal metric table, a
# label, and which thresholding scheme it belongs to. The family is declared
# here, once, and the false discovery rate correction is applied within it.
METRICS <- data.frame(
  col = c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "peak_bui", "mean_isi", "mean_dmc", "peak_dc",
          "n_ffmc_gt91", "n_fwi_gt19", "n_fwi_gt30",
          "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95", "n_isi_p95"),
  label = c("Mean FWI", "Seasonal severity rating", "Peak BUI",
            "Mean ISI", "Mean DMC", "Peak DC",
            "Days FFMC > 91", "Days FWI > 19", "Days FWI > 30",
            "Days FWI above own 90th percentile",
            "Days FWI above own 95th percentile",
            "Days ISI above own 95th percentile"),
  scheme = c("level", "level", "level", "level", "level", "level",
             "absolute", "absolute", "absolute",
             "relative", "relative", "relative"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Trends are estimated per station and per series, then combined, rather than on
# a basin average, because the set of reporting stations changes between seasons
# and a basin average would move when a station joins or leaves.
trend_rows <- list()
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      d <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == stn, ]
      d <- d[is.finite(d[[m]]), ]
      if (nrow(d) < 15) next
      tt <- trend_test(d$year, d[[m]])
      tt$series <- s; tt$metric <- m; tt$station <- stn
      tt$mdt <- minimum_detectable_trend(d$year, d[[m]])
      trend_rows[[length(trend_rows) + 1]] <- tt
    }
  }
}
trends <- do.call(rbind, trend_rows)
if (is.null(trends) || !nrow(trends))
  stop("No station has the 15 seasons the trend estimator requires. ",
       "Kept station-seasons: ", n_kept, " over ", n_seasons, " seasons. ",
       "Delete the weather record and the daily series and render again ",
       "to rebuild them over the full archive.")
# The family is the twelve metrics within one series at one station.
trends$q <- ave(trends$p_corrected,
                paste(trends$series, trends$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(trends, file.path(outputs, "trend-estimates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Theil-Sen slopes per season for each seasonal metric under each series, pooled across stations as the median station slope, with the range across stations. Significance is Mann-Kendall with the Hamed and Rao variance correction; the count is of stations at which the false discovery rate adjusted p value falls below 0.05 within that station's twelve-metric family. The minimum detectable trend is the slope this record could resolve at 90 per cent power."
tr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, list(trends$series, trends$metric),
                                  drop = TRUE), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    Stations = nrow(d),
    `Median slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Slope range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE),
                            max(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Min detectable` = round(median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
tr <- tr[order(match(tr$Metric, METRICS$label), tr$Series), ]
rownames(tr) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tr, size = 8, numeric = "center")
```

The absolute and relative extreme-day counts are the panels the second question turned on, under the prediction that the absolute counts separate between series and the relative counts do not."
show <- METRICS$col
# Generous bottom margin and tightened axis title placement: at four rows on one

  for (s in names(SERIES)) {

    # The line carries the reported estimate, the median of the per-station
    # Theil-Sen slopes in the trend table, through the median point of the
    # station means. A line fitted to the station means would be the basin
    # average the trend chunk avoids, which drops when a cooler station joins.
    sl <- median(trends$slope[trends$series == s & trends$metric == m], na.rm = TRUE)
    abline(a = median(a$x) - sl * median(a$year), b = sl, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)

```{r}
#| label: trend-reading
#| output: false
# The direction and strength of the trend picture, computed rather than eyeballed
# off the table, so the sentence below cannot say something the numbers do not.
tr_up <- sum(trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_n <- sum(is.finite(trends$slope))
tr_sig <- sum(trends$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_sig_up <- sum(trends$q < 0.05 & trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
# What the autocorrelation correction changed, in tests that would pass on the
# uncorrected variance, corrected within the same families as the reported q
# values, each station's twelve metrics within a series.
would_pass <- sum(unlist(lapply(split(trends$p_uncorrected, list(trends$series, trends$station), drop = TRUE),
  function(p) p.adjust(p, "BH"))) < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
infl <- median(trends$n_over_nstar, na.rm = TRUE)
# The two extremes among the extreme-day counts, which share the unit days per
# season, so that the paragraph names its highest and lowest cases rather than
# reporting only a count of how many passed.
day_tr <- trends[trends$metric %in% METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme != "level"], ]
hi <- day_tr[which.max(day_tr$slope), ]
lo <- day_tr[which.min(day_tr$slope), ]
# The twelve metrics as they read inside a sentence, where a table label with
# its symbol would not.
METRIC_PROSE <- c(
  mean_fwi    = "mean Fire Weather Index",
  ssr         = "seasonal severity rating",
  peak_bui    = "peak Buildup Index",
  mean_isi    = "mean Initial Spread Index",
  mean_dmc    = "mean Duff Moisture Code",
  peak_dc     = "peak Drought Code",
  n_ffmc_gt91 = "days with a Fine Fuel Moisture Code above 91",
  n_fwi_gt19  = "days with a Fire Weather Index above 19",
  n_fwi_gt30  = "days with a Fire Weather Index above 30",
  n_fwi_p90   = "days with a Fire Weather Index above the series' own 90th percentile",
  n_fwi_p95   = "days with a Fire Weather Index above the series' own 95th percentile",
  n_isi_p95   = "days with an Initial Spread Index above the series' own 95th percentile")
name_case <- function(r) sprintf("at %s, in %s under %s",
  station_prose(r$station), METRIC_PROSE[[r$metric]], unname(SERIES_PROSE[r$series]))
slope_case <- function(r) sprintf("%+.2f days per season, 95 per cent interval %+.2f to %+.2f, q = %s",
  r$slope, r$lower, r$upper, ifelse(r$q < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", r$q)))
# Where the trends that passed sit, by station, so that the paragraph names the
# stations rather than leaving the count pooled across them.
sig_station <- sort(tapply(trends$q < 0.05, trends$station, sum, na.rm = TRUE),
                    decreasing = TRUE)
top <- names(sig_station)[1]
top_miss <- unique(trends$metric[trends$station == top & !(trends$q < 0.05)])
top_phrase <- if (length(top_miss)) {
  sprintf("%s, every metric except %s", station_prose(top),
          paste(METRIC_PROSE[top_miss], collapse = " and "))
} else sprintf("%s, every metric", station_prose(top))
min_q_station <- tapply(trends$q, trends$station, min, na.rm = TRUE)
none <- names(sig_station)[sig_station == 0]
none <- none[order(min_q_station[none])]
none_stations <- paste(station_prose(none), collapse = " or ")
none_q <- paste(sprintf("%.3f", min_q_station[none]), collapse = " and ")
# Where the test and the interval disagree, because they answer different
# questions and a reader will set them side by side.
n_sig_inc0 <- sum(trends$q < 0.05 & trends$lower <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_nonsig_excl0 <- sum(trends$q >= 0.05 & (trends$lower > 0 | trends$upper < 0), na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: neighbour-check
#| output: false
# Whether the station that carried most of the passing trends rose relative to
# its neighbours. The difference between two stations' seasonal means removes
# whatever the basin's weather did to both, so a trend in the difference points
# to the station or its surroundings rather than to the basin. Same estimator
# and test as the trends themselves, on the seasons the two stations share.
nb_rows <- list()
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  a <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == top, c("year", "mean_fwi")]
  for (st in setdiff(unique(trends$station), top)) {
    b <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == st, c("year", "mean_fwi")]
    d <- merge(a, b, by = "year", suffixes = c("_top", "_nb"))
    d <- d[order(d$year), ]
    dd <- d$mean_fwi_top - d$mean_fwi_nb
    mk <- modifiedmk::mmkh(as.vector(dd))
    nb_rows[[length(nb_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      series = s, station = st, n = nrow(d), slope = theil_sen(d$year, dd),
      tau = unname(mk["Tau"]), p = unname(mk["new P-value"]))
  }
}
neighbour <- do.call(rbind, nb_rows)
write.csv(neighbour, file.path(outputs, "neighbour-differences.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
# The neighbour named in the prose is the one sharing most seasons with the
# station, under S1.
nb_main <- neighbour[neighbour$series == "s1", ]
nb_main <- nb_main[which.max(nb_main$n), ]
nb_all_up <- all(neighbour$slope > 0)
```

Across the study window, trends were tested at the `r length(unique(trends$station))` stations with at least 15 usable seasons. Of the `r tr_n` station, series and metric combinations, `r tr_up` had a positive Theil-Sen slope (@tbl-trends, @fig-trends). The Mann-Kendall test was run with the Hamed and Rao variance correction and the false discovery rate correction within each station's twelve-metric family. After both corrections, `r tr_sig` combinations had a q value below 0.05, `r if (tr_sig_up == tr_sig) "all" else tr_sig_up` of them positive. Of those, `r sig_station[[1]]` were at `r top_phrase`, and `r sig_station[[2]]` at `r station_prose(names(sig_station)[2])`. None was at `r none_stations`, where the smallest q values were `r none_q`. Of the `r tr_sig`, `r n_sig_inc0` had a bootstrap interval that included zero, and `r n_nonsig_excl0` of the other `r tr_n - tr_sig` combinations had an interval that excluded it. The median ratio of the nominal to the effective sample size was `r sprintf("%.2f", infl)`, where the effective size was the number of independent seasons the correlated record was worth. On the uncorrected variance, `r would_pass` combinations would have passed the same threshold. The extreme-day counts shared the unit days per season, so their slopes could be ranked. The steepest rise was `r name_case(hi)`. Its slope was `r slope_case(hi)`. The `r if (lo$slope < 0) "steepest fall" else "shallowest rise"` was `r name_case(lo)`. Its slope was `r slope_case(lo)`. The mean Fire Weather Index at `r station_prose(top)` was also compared with each other station's on the seasons they shared. Against `r station_prose(nb_main$station)`, the station sharing most seasons with it, the difference rose `r sprintf("%.2f", nb_main$slope)` units per season under S1, Kendall tau `r sprintf("%.2f", nb_main$tau)`, uncorrected p = `r sprintf("%.3f", nb_main$p)`. Across the three series and three neighbours, the slopes of the differences were `r if (nb_all_up) "all positive" else "not all positive"` and the p values ranged from `r sprintf("%.3f", min(neighbour$p))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(neighbour$p))`.

## Version Dependence

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-compute
#| output: false
CONTRASTS <- list(
  c("s1", "s2", "Version change, input held at 13:00"),
  c("s2", "s3", "Input resolution change, version held at FWI2025"),
  c("s1", "s3", "Operational migration, both changes")
)

diff_rows <- list()
for (cn in CONTRASTS) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      a <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[1] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      b <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[2] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      w <- merge(a, b, by = "year", suffixes = c(".a", ".b"))
      names(w)[2:3] <- c("a", "b")
      if (nrow(w) < 15) next
      sd_ <- slope_difference(w)
      sd_$contrast <- cn[3]; sd_$metric <- m; sd_$station <- stn
      sd_$scheme <- METRICS$scheme[i]
      diff_rows[[length(diff_rows) + 1]] <- sd_
    }
  }
}
sdiff <- do.call(rbind, diff_rows)
if (is.null(sdiff) || !nrow(sdiff))
  stop("No station-series pair has the 15 paired seasons the bootstrap requires.")
# The family here is the twelve metrics within one contrast at one station: one
# station's answer to one of the three questions the design asks.
sdiff$q <- ave(sdiff$p_two_sided, paste(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(sdiff, file.path(outputs, "slope-differences.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

#| label: tbl-slopediff
#| tbl-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series, by metric and contrast, pooled across stations as the median. Intervals are paired moving-block bootstrap percentile intervals over 4,000 resamples of blocks of consecutive seasons, which preserves both the dependence between series that share a weather record and the serial correlation within each. Stations excluding zero counts the stations whose own interval does not contain zero; the last column applies the Benjamini and Hochberg correction within each station's twelve-metric family for that contrast."
sd_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(sdiff, list(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$metric), drop = TRUE), function(d) {
    data.frame(
      Contrast = d$contrast[1],
      Scheme = d$scheme[1],
      Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
      Stations = nrow(d),
      `Median difference` = round(median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      `Stations excluding zero` = sum(d$lower > 0 | d$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      check.names = FALSE)
  }))
sd_tab <- sd_tab[order(match(sd_tab$Contrast, vapply(CONTRASTS, `[`, "", 3)),
                       match(sd_tab$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(sd_tab) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(sd_tab, size = 8)

```{r}
#| label: fig-slopediff
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series for the six extreme-day counts, which all measure days per season and therefore share one axis. Points are station estimates, bars are paired moving-block bootstrap 95 per cent intervals over 4,000 resamples of blocks of consecutive seasons. Red marks the three absolute thresholds and blue the three thresholds internal to each series. The prediction under test is that the red points separate from zero and the blue ones do not. The six level metrics are omitted from this figure because the seasonal severity rating and the Drought Code are measured on scales two orders of magnitude larger and would compress everything else to a point; they are in the preceding table."
# Only the metrics measured in days per season are drawn, so one x axis means the
# same thing everywhere on the figure. A common range across the three panels
# keeps the contrasts comparable, and the labels are drawn once on the left.
DAY_METRICS <- METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme %in% c("absolute", "relative")]
sd_plot <- sdiff[sdiff$metric %in% DAY_METRICS, ]
sd_plot$mi <- match(sd_plot$metric, METRICS$col)
xr <- range(c(sd_plot$lower, sd_plot$upper, 0), na.rm = TRUE)

# The left outer margin is sized from the longest row label, so that a longer
# metric name cannot clip the labels as a fixed width did on 2026-10-26.
lab_w <- max(nchar(paste0(METRICS$label[sd_plot$mi], ", ", sd_plot$station)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), oma = c(1.6, 0.31 * lab_w, 0, 0), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (k in seq_along(CONTRASTS)) {
  cn <- CONTRASTS[[k]]
  d <- sd_plot[sd_plot$contrast == cn[3], ]
  par(mar = c(2.6, 0.6, 3.4, 0.6))
  if (!nrow(d)) { plot.new(); next }
  d <- d[order(d$mi, d$station), ]
  y <- seq_len(nrow(d))
  plot(NA, xlim = xr, ylim = c(0.5, max(y) + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
       xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = paste(strwrap(cn[3], 24), collapse = "\n"), cex.main = 0.95)
  abline(v = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
  segments(d$lower, y, d$upper, y, col = "grey35")

         col = ifelse(d$scheme == "absolute", "#943126", "#1B4F72"))

    axis(2, at = y, labels = paste0(METRICS$label[d$mi], ", ", d$station),
         las = 1, cex.axis = 0.7, tick = FALSE, line = -0.3, outer = TRUE)
}
# One axis title under all three panels, because the panels share the axis and
# three titles side by side ran into one another.
mtext("Slope difference, days per season", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.3, cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-reading
#| output: false
# The hypothesis has a specific shape: absolute-threshold counts should separate
# between series and relative-threshold counts should not. That shape is scored
# here as two rates, so the sentence below reports what the numbers show rather
# than what the hypothesis predicted.
score <- function(contrast, scheme) {
  d <- sdiff[sdiff$contrast == contrast & sdiff$scheme == scheme, ]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(c(n = 0, sig = 0, rate = NA_real_, med = NA_real_))
  sig <- sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  c(n = nrow(d), sig = sig, rate = 100 * sig / nrow(d),
    med = median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE))
}
ver_label <- CONTRASTS[[1]][3]
inp_label <- CONTRASTS[[2]][3]
mig_label <- CONTRASTS[[3]][3]
sc <- rbind(
  `version, absolute`   = score(ver_label, "absolute"),
  `version, relative`   = score(ver_label, "relative"),
  `input, absolute`     = score(inp_label, "absolute"),
  `input, relative`     = score(inp_label, "relative"),
  `migration, absolute` = score(mig_label, "absolute"),
  `migration, relative` = score(mig_label, "relative"))
sc <- as.data.frame(sc)
write.csv(sc, file.path(outputs, "hypothesis-scoring.csv"))

# The resolution of the difference test, so that a null is readable. The half
# width of the bootstrap interval is the smallest difference this record could
# have separated from zero at each station and metric.
sdiff$halfwidth <- (sdiff$upper - sdiff$lower) / 2
res_abs <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "absolute"], na.rm = TRUE)
res_rel <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "relative"], na.rm = TRUE)
n_any_sig <- sum(sdiff$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
# The largest difference among the metrics measured in days per season, named
# with its contrast, so that the null is reported beside its nearest case.
day_sd <- sdiff[sdiff$scheme != "level", ]
big <- day_sd[which.max(abs(day_sd$difference)), ]
big_i <- match(big$contrast, vapply(CONTRASTS, `[`, "", 3))
big_a <- toupper(CONTRASTS[[big_i]][1])
big_b <- toupper(CONTRASTS[[big_i]][2])
CONTRAST_PROSE <- c("version change", "input resolution change", "migration")
big_case <- sprintf("at %s, in %s under the %s", station_prose(big$station),
                    METRIC_PROSE[[big$metric]], CONTRAST_PROSE[big_i])

abs_rate <- sc["migration, absolute", "rate"]
rel_rate <- sc["migration, relative", "rate"]
verdict <- if (!is.finite(abs_rate) || !is.finite(rel_rate)) {
  "could not be scored"
} else if (abs_rate == 0 && rel_rate == 0) {
  "divergence under neither scheme, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism"
} else if (abs_rate > rel_rate) {
  "the pattern the mechanism predicted"
} else if (abs_rate > 0) {
  "divergence under both schemes, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism"
} else {
  "divergence under the percentile scheme alone, the opposite of the pattern the mechanism predicted"
}
```

Across the study window, the migration contrast, S1 against S3, gave `r verdict`. The absolute-threshold metrics gave a slope difference excluding zero at `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of station and metric combinations against `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, relative", "rate"])` per cent for the relative-threshold metrics (@tbl-slopediff, @fig-slopediff). Across all `r nrow(sdiff)` station, metric and contrast combinations, `r if (n_any_sig == 0) "none" else n_any_sig` gave a slope difference with a corrected p value below 0.05. The smallest uncorrected p value was `r sprintf("%.3f", min(sdiff$p_two_sided, na.rm = TRUE))`. The largest difference among the day-count metrics was `r big_case`. There the slope under `r big_b` was `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(big$difference))` days per season `r if (big$difference < 0) "below" else "above"` that under `r big_a`, 95 per cent interval `r sprintf("%+.2f", big$lower)` to `r sprintf("%+.2f", big$upper)`, q = `r sprintf("%.3f", big$q)`. The resolution of the test was the median half width of the bootstrap intervals on the slope differences. It was `r sprintf("%.3f", res_abs)` days per season for the absolute-threshold metrics and `r sprintf("%.3f", res_rel)` for the relative ones. Over the `r yr_last - yr_first` season window that was `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", res_rel * (yr_last - yr_first))` days respectively. The migration contrast was then split into its two halves. The version change alone, S1 against S2, gave `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["version, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of absolute-metric slope differences excluding zero. The input resolution change alone, S2 against S3, gave `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["input, absolute", "rate"])` per cent. The median differences were `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["version, absolute", "med"])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["input, absolute", "med"])` days per season respectively against `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["migration, absolute", "med"])` for the two together.

## Ignition Skill

```{r}
#| label: ignition-compute
#| output: false
mod_dat <- merge(basin, ign_daily, by = c("date", "year", "doy"))
mod_dat <- mod_dat[format(mod_dat$date, "%m") %in% c("05", "06", "07", "08", "09"), ]

SKILL_RESPONSES <- c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")

RESPONSES <- c(n_lightning_all = "Lightning, no size limit",
               n_person_all = "Person, no size limit",
               n_total_all = "All causes, no size limit",
               n_total_ge1ha = "All causes, at least 1 ha",
               n_total_ge4ha = "All causes, at least 4 ha")

ign_rows <- list()
for (r in names(RESPONSES)) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    if (!dcol %in% names(mod_dat)) next
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, r, dcol, extra = "n_stations"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    # Held-out skill is computed only for the two responses the comparison
    # between series is read from. It refits the model once per season, so
    # running it on all five responses costs several hundred fits for numbers
    # the text does not use, and the cost is reported rather than hidden.
    sk <- if (r %in% SKILL_RESPONSES)
      tryCatch(loso_skill(mod_dat, r, dcol), error = function(e) NULL) else NULL
    # Wald interval on the danger coefficient rather than a profile likelihood
    # one. Profiling a negative binomial with a factor per season means refitting
    # once per grid point per model, which dominated the render, and the two
    # agree closely at this sample size. The interval is reported as Wald.
    se <- summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 2]
    ci <- coef(m)[".x"] + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
    ign_rows[[length(ign_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      coef = unname(coef(m)[".x"]),
      lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
      p = summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 4],
      theta = m$theta,
      loso_loglik = if (is.null(sk)) NA_real_ else sk$mean_loglik,
      n_days = nrow(mod_dat))
  }
}
ign_res <- do.call(rbind, ign_rows)
write.csv(ign_res, file.path(outputs, "ignition-models.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ignition
#| tbl-cap: "Negative binomial models of daily ignition counts on daily basin Fire Weather Index, over the 1 May to 30 September window, with season as a fixed effect, two annual harmonics in day of year, and the number of contributing stations. The coefficient is the log change in expected count per unit of Fire Weather Index, identified from within-season variation only. Held-out log likelihood is the mean per day under leave-one-season-out refitting; larger is better, and the comparison between series rather than its absolute value is the quantity of interest. It is computed for the lightning and all-cause responses only, because those are the two the text compares and each refits the model once per season."
it <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[ign_res$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[ign_res$series]),
  `Coefficient` = round(ign_res$coef, 4),
  `95% Wald interval` = sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", ign_res$lower, ign_res$upper),
  `Rate ratio per 10 FWI` = round(exp(10 * ign_res$coef), 2),
  `Held-out log likelihood` = round(ign_res$loso_loglik, 4),
  check.names = FALSE)
it <- it[order(match(it$Response, unname(RESPONSES)), it$Series), ]
rownames(it) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(it)

```{r}
#| label: ignition-prose
#| output: false
best <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all", ]
best <- best[order(-best$loso_loglik), ]
skill_gap <- diff(range(best$loso_loglik))

# Does the danger term survive at every size threshold, and does it separate the
# lightning series from the person-caused control? The control matters: human
# ignition tracks population and access, so a danger signal appearing equally in
# both would point to a shared confounder rather than to fuel moisture.
sig_by_response <- tapply(ign_res$p, ign_res$response, function(p) sum(p < 0.05))
rr <- function(resp, s) {
  v <- ign_res$coef[ign_res$response == resp & ign_res$series == s]
  if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else exp(10 * v)
}
rr_light <- rr("n_lightning_all", "s3")
rr_person <- rr("n_person_all", "s3")
rr_ci <- function(resp, s) {
  r <- ign_res[ign_res$response == resp & ign_res$series == s, ]
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(10 * r$lower), exp(10 * r$upper))
}
p_light <- setNames(ign_res$p[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all"],
                    ign_res$series[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all"])
# The same held-out comparison for all causes, so that the lightning gap is
# read beside the other response the models scored.
best_all <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_total_all", ]
best_all <- best_all[order(-best_all$loso_loglik), ]
skill_gap_all <- diff(range(best_all$loso_loglik))
same_order <- best_all$series[1] == best$series[1] &&
  best_all$series[nrow(best_all)] == best$series[nrow(best)]
order_phrase <- if (same_order) "with the same series first and last" else
  sprintf("with %s first and %s last", SERIES_PROSE[[best_all$series[1]]],
          SERIES_PROSE[[best_all$series[nrow(best_all)]]])
```

Over the summer window, the danger term in the negative binomial ignition models was the coefficient on the daily basin Fire Weather Index. It was positive with a p value below 0.05 for `r sum(ign_res$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r nrow(ign_res)` response and series combinations (@tbl-ignition). The person-caused response was significant under every series and the lightning response only under FWI1987, with p = `r sprintf("%.3f", p_light[["s2"]])` under S2 and `r sprintf("%.3f", p_light[["s3"]])` under S3. Under FWI2025 on hourly weather, ten units of Fire Weather Index multiplied the expected daily person-caused count by `r sprintf("%.2f", rr_person)`, 95 per cent interval `r rr_ci("n_person_all", "s3")`. The same ten units multiplied the expected daily lightning count by `r sprintf("%.2f", rr_light)`, interval `r rr_ci("n_lightning_all", "s3")`. Under FWI1987 the fitted dispersion parameter was `r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all"][1])` for the lightning series against `r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_person_all"][1])` for the person-caused one, a smaller value meaning more clustered counts.

The difference in predictive skill between series, the third question, was small. On held-out seasons, the three series differed by `r sprintf("%.4f", skill_gap)` in mean log likelihood per day for lightning ignitions. `r unname(SERIES_PROSE[best$series[1]])` was first at `r sprintf("%.4f", best$loso_loglik[1])` and `r unname(SERIES_PROSE[best$series[nrow(best)]])` last at `r sprintf("%.4f", best$loso_loglik[nrow(best)])`. Over the `r format(best$n_days[1], big.mark = ",")` days in the window that was a total of about `r sprintf("%.1f", skill_gap * best$n_days[1])` log likelihood units. For all causes the gap was `r sprintf("%.4f", skill_gap_all)` per day, `r order_phrase`.

```{r}
#| label: stationarity
#| output: false
# Is the danger to ignition relationship stationary? The test is an interaction
# between the danger term and season number. Season is already a fixed effect,
# so the interaction asks whether the within-season slope changes over the
# record, which is a different question from whether the intercept does.
stat_rows <- list()
for (r in c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    d <- mod_dat
    d$.yc <- d$year - mean(d$year)
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(d, r, dcol, extra = "I(.x * .yc)"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    cf <- summary(m)$coefficients
    nm <- grep("I\\(.x", rownames(cf), value = TRUE)[1]
    stat_rows[[length(stat_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      interaction = cf[nm, 1], se = cf[nm, 2], p = cf[nm, 4])
  }
}
stationarity <- do.call(rbind, stat_rows)
write.csv(stationarity, file.path(outputs, "stationarity-tests.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
n_stat_sig <- sum(stationarity$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Across the record, the interaction between the danger term and season number tested whether the danger to ignition relationship changed with time. `r if (n_stat_sig == 0) "None" else n_stat_sig` of the `r nrow(stationarity)` interaction terms had a p value below 0.05, and the p values ranged from `r sprintf("%.3f", min(stationarity$p))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(stationarity$p))`.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: discussion-numbers
#| output: false
# The basin's percentile-day trend beside the published global rate, as a share,
# so that the sentence states the comparison and not two numbers side by side.
rel95_season <- median(trends$slope[trends$metric == "n_fwi_p95"], na.rm = TRUE)
rel95_decade <- 10 * rel95_season
GLOBAL_P95_DECADE <- 2.65   # Matteo et al. (2025), days per decade over 1980 to 2023
rel95_share <- 100 * rel95_decade / GLOBAL_P95_DECADE
# The station that carried most passing trends against its named neighbour, on
# the median slope of the mean Fire Weather Index.
fwi_slope_station <- tapply(trends$slope[trends$metric == "mean_fwi"],
                            trends$station[trends$metric == "mean_fwi"], median, na.rm = TRUE)
# Which neighbours the station pulled away from under S1, named, so that a flat
# difference is reported beside the rising ones.
nb_s1 <- neighbour[neighbour$series == "s1", ]
nb_up <- nb_s1$station[nb_s1$p < 0.05]
nb_flat <- nb_s1$station[nb_s1$p >= 0.05]
nb_phrase <- if (!length(nb_flat)) {
  sprintf("against every neighbour, %s", paste(station_prose(nb_up), collapse = " and "))
} else if (!length(nb_up)) {
  "against none of the three neighbours at an uncorrected p below 0.05"
} else sprintf("against %s, at an uncorrected p below 0.05, and not against %s",
               paste(station_prose(nb_up), collapse = " and "),
               paste(station_prose(nb_flat), collapse = " or "))
# Direction words for the prose, computed so that a sentence cannot assert a sign
# the numbers do not show. Rows 3 to 5 of shift are the spread index and the two
# slow codes.
slow_phrase <- if (all(shift$version[4:5] > 0)) {
  "the Duff Moisture Code and the Drought Code to the dry side"
} else if (all(shift$version[4:5] < 0)) {
  "the Duff Moisture Code and the Drought Code to the wet side"
} else "the Duff Moisture Code and the Drought Code in opposite directions"
reverse_phrase <- if (sign(shift$input[1]) == -sign(shift$version[1]) &&
                      sign(shift$input[2]) == -sign(shift$version[2])) {
  "The input change did the reverse."
} else "The input change did not simply reverse it."
# Slope differences excluding zero among the four metrics added for the rewritten
# components, over all three contrasts.
new_metric_names <- c("mean_isi", "mean_dmc", "peak_dc", "n_isi_p95",
                      "Mean ISI", "Mean DMC", "Peak DC", "Days ISI above own 95th percentile")
sd_new <- sdiff[sdiff$metric %in% new_metric_names, ]
stopifnot(nrow(sd_new) == 4 * length(unique(sdiff$station)) * length(unique(sdiff$contrast)))
n_excl_new <- sum(sd_new$lower > 0 | sd_new$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
excl_word <- if (n_excl_new == 0) "None" else as.character(n_excl_new)
# Where the two changes oppose, what survives is the residual, and how much
# survives is the whole point. Cancellation is measured as the migration shift
# relative to the larger of the two component shifts.
same_sign <- function(i) sign(shift$version[i]) == sign(shift$input[i])
ffmc_word <- if (same_sign(1)) "compounded" else "opposed one another"
fwi_word <- if (same_sign(2)) "compounded" else "opposed one another"
residual <- function(i) {
  abs(shift$migration[i]) / max(abs(shift$version[i]), abs(shift$input[i]))
}
ffmc_res <- residual(1); fwi_res <- residual(2)
bigger <- function(i) if (abs(shift$version[i]) > abs(shift$input[i]))
  "the version change" else "the input resolution change"
# The slope a line would read from a step of the migration's size placed at
# mid-record, under the estimator the study used, so that the consequence of
# joining a count series across the change is a number rather than a warning.
yrs <- yr_first:yr_last
step <- c(rep(0, floor(length(yrs) / 2)), rep(shift$migration[1], ceiling(length(yrs) / 2)))
step_slope <- theil_sen(yrs, step)
step_window <- step_slope * (yr_last - yr_first)
step_pct <- 100 * step_slope / median(trends$slope[trends$metric == "n_ffmc_gt91"], na.rm = TRUE)
```

Over `r yr_first` to `r yr_last` in the Okanagan basin of British Columbia, the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System was run as three series on one weather record. One pair of series isolated the version change and the other the change in input resolution. The revision moved the count of extreme days and moved no trend this record could resolve. The predicted divergence in slope appeared under neither thresholding scheme, which refuted the mechanism, and the three series were barely distinguishable in their skill at predicting daily ignitions.

## Trends

Over `r yr_first` to `r yr_last`, days above the series' own 95th percentile rose by a median of `r sprintf("%.2f", rel95_season)` per season across stations and series, `r sprintf("%.1f", rel95_decade)` days per decade. Worldwide over 1980 to 2023 in a reanalysis, the same count "increased by 2.65 days per decade" [@matteo2025challenges]. The basin's rate was `r sprintf("%.0f", rel95_share)` per cent of the global one, from one basin's stations rather than a global grid.

Of the `r tr_sig` trends with q below 0.05, `r sig_station[[1]]` were at `r station_prose(top)`. There the median slope of the mean Fire Weather Index was `r sprintf("%.2f", fwi_slope_station[[top]])` units per season, against `r sprintf("%.2f", fwi_slope_station[[nb_main$station]])` at `r station_prose(nb_main$station)`. The difference between two stations' seasonal means removed whatever the basin's weather did to both. A trend in that difference therefore pointed to the station or its surroundings rather than to the basin. Under S1 the difference rose `r nb_phrase`. Whatever moved one series moved all three, so the comparison between series was unaffected. The sensor history was unavailable, so a change at the site could not be separated from a local change in the weather.

The Mann-Kendall test asked whether a series rose, and the block bootstrap asked how far the slope could lie under resampled seasons. Of the `r tr_sig` trends that passed the test, `r n_sig_inc0` had an interval that included zero. The count of trends therefore rested on the test and the size of each on its interval, and the two were not interchangeable.

## Version and Input

The two changes were large and pointed opposite ways, so a straight comparison of FWI1987 against FWI2025 would have been uninterpretable. On the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 the two `r ffmc_word` and `r bigger(1)` won. On the count above a Fire Weather Index of 19 they `r fwi_word` almost exactly, and the migration netted `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fwi_res)` per cent of the larger component. That near cancellation was a coincidence of two large effects at one place. It was not to be expected at a site with a different diurnal range, the difference in temperature and humidity between night and day.

The two changes did not move the counts in the directions expected. In the Northwest Territories, the hourly code of 1977 and the diurnally adjusted code had both "consistently overestimated the minimum moisture content" of needle litter and feathermoss on dry days [@beck2004diurnal, pp. 213, 218]. FWI2025 cut in half the time lag of the 1977 hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code, so that fine fuels dried faster [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 18]. It nonetheless `r up_down(shift$version[1])` the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 and `r up_down(shift$version[2])` the count above a Fire Weather Index of 19. `r reverse_phrase` At five stations in the Alps over 1951 to 2010, "Regional differences were highest for the FFMC, followed by the DMC and the DC, and could be attributed to the time lag of different forest soil layers" [@wastl2013large, abstract]. Faster drying should therefore have acted most strongly on the Fine Fuel Moisture Code and the counts built from it, which this record did not show. @rodrigues2020identifying noted of the Fire Weather Index that "a same result may be produced by different combinations of weather variables" [@rodrigues2020identifying, abstract]. Two changes acting on different parts of the calculation could therefore offset in the combined index while remaining visible in its parts.

At fixed 13:00 input, the version change moved `r slow_phrase`. The report had expected its cumulative rain thresholds to "err to the dry side of fuel moisture" on "days where two rainfall events are spaced apart by more than six hours" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 21]. On days with one main rain event, it expected "little to no difference" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 21]. Pathway C placed each day's rain in the first hour after sunrise, so the rain thresholds could explain little of the rise at fixed input. The migration left the Duff Moisture Code `r up_down(shift$migration[4], "higher", "lower")` and the Drought Code `r up_down(shift$migration[5], "higher", "lower")` than under FWI1987. The mean Initial Spread Index `r up_down(shift$version[3], "rose", "fell")` under the version change despite the new wind cap. That was consistent with a 16:00 daily value taken nearer the afternoon peak than the 13:00 observation. `r excl_word` of the four metrics added for the rewritten components had a slope difference that excluded zero in any contrast.

At Camden, New South Wales, three fire danger systems were compared on thirteen years of station data, each at its own observation time [@matthews2009comparison]. Differences in how each took in the weather "cancelled out some of the differences in structure" [@matthews2009comparison, p. 41]. The version and input effects did the same here for days above a Fire Weather Index of 19. That study followed no trend through the change. The one measured effect of input timing on a slope was the 0.22 to 0.39 days per decade by which daily aggregates inflated a global extreme-day trend [@matteo2025challenges]. Over this window that would have amounted to `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.22 * (yr_last - yr_first) / 10)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.39 * (yr_last - yr_first) / 10)` days, against the `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` days this record could resolve. The null slope result therefore bounded the effect rather than excluding it.

The clearest difference between the two FWI2025 series was not in any level but in the burning window. Both series followed the report's own procedures, so an agency that migrated to FWI2025 while still supplying a 13:00 observation would receive outputs computed from an assumed diurnal curve. The report had said as much, warning that "any weather estimate, including those derived from our methods, involves inherent assumptions" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 30]. A daily index could not say when the peak arrived or how long it lasted. The report noted that its hour of peak burn "represents a mathematical maximum and does not provide an indication of how sharp or flat that 'peak' is" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 27]. It added that "the width of the burning window on a particular day may also be a useful addition" [@cffdg2025fwi2025, p. 27]. The hourly series reported both without predicting ignitions better.

The small difference in ignition skill between series was consistent with comparisons of danger indices against fire records elsewhere. In Mediterranean France, "the Canadian FWI remains the most skillful indicator among the tested indices" [@castelclavera2025comparative, abstract]. The same study found that "relying solely on fire-weather indices is insufficient" and that "the inclusion of spatial and seasonal effects in the models is crucial" [@castelclavera2025comparative, abstract]. The models here included the seasonal effect, and a model of one basin mean had no spatial effect to include. Across 11 regions from the European Alps to the Mediterranean basin, models that ranked fire occurrence well could still perform poorly on burned area [@bekar2023integrating]. The ignition counts tested here therefore could not show whether the three series would differ on area burned.

## Published Trends

Because the migration changed no estimated trend at any station under either thresholding scheme, the consequence for the published record rested on the level result alone. A series of percentile exceedances was unaffected by the version change, because the threshold moved with the distribution. In the United States system at Missoula, Montana, over 1999 to 2008, changing the fuel model moved the 97th percentile of the Energy Release Component from 69 to 39 [@heinsch2009percentiles, p. 4]. With the classes set at percentiles, "a similar number of days fall in each class" under either fuel model [@heinsch2009percentiles, p. 4]. A series of counts above a fixed danger class carried the level shift, and so did the seasonal severity rating, which summed a function of the index over a season. Joined across the change, such a series would carry a step at the join, which a fitted line would read as trend. A step of `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$migration[1]))` days per season at mid-record, the migration's size at a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, gave a Theil-Sen slope of `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(step_slope))` days per season. That was `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(step_window))` days over the window and `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(step_pct))` per cent of the slope observed in that count. An archive of operational index values could hold such a join with no record of it. In mainland Portugal, @nunes2026ignitions took the Fire Weather Index stored with each fire record of 2001 to 2024, without recalculating it [@nunes2026ignitions, p. 3]. The "exact procedure used to assign daily FWI to individual ignitions could not be independently reconstructed" [@nunes2026ignitions, p. 12]. Of the trends cited here, the extreme days of @matteo2025challenges were percentile exceedances, which the version change left unchanged. The spread days of @jain2017seasonlength, the threshold days of @wastl2012climate and the mean index of @queen2025fingerprint were fixed thresholds or levels, which it moved. The fire weather days of @richardson2022global were counted on the McArthur Forest Fire Danger Index, which the version change did not touch [@richardson2022global, p. 7]. A percentile trend was portable across the version change only when its reference period was stated and kept fixed, with the base-period bias corrected where the record ran beyond it [@zhang2005percentile]. Fixed classes were already regional and tied to the period that calibrated them. In 1977, British Columbia's Class V needed a Fire Weather Index above 46 and a Buildup Index above 90 in the region holding the Thompson-Okanagan valleys [@lawson1977bc, pp. 14–15]. In its coast and wet interior region, every day above a Fire Weather Index of 30 was Class V [@lawson1977bc, p. 15]. In Ontario, the classes were set so that the Extreme class held "2% of fire season days" [@hanes2021classes, abstract]. By 2021, modifications "would still be warranted as the values no longer reflect the original frequency of occurrence expectations", even if Ontario kept its existing classes [@hanes2021classes, abstract]. In Canada's forests over 2001 to 2021, the Fire Weather Index below which half the area burned was 20.1, with a standard deviation of 0.5 [@wang2025spread, p. 5]. By ecozone, the same threshold ran from 12.9 in the Taiga Cordillera to 25.3 in the Montane Cordillera, with standard deviations of 1.9 and 3.0 [@wang2025spread, p. 6].

Nothing here showed the published trends to be wrong, but they were statements about FWI1987. Restating them under FWI2025 would change some by an amount set by the metric's definition rather than by the weather. A level shift that did not alter the relative change had been reported before in this index. @quilcaille2023fire found that computing the Fire Weather Index from mean rather than minimum humidity reduced it "by about −33 % (June) above 20° N" [@quilcaille2023fire, p. 2162]. The reduction was "roughly identical during the fire seasons across the planet, be it over 1994–2014 or 2081–2100" [@quilcaille2023fire, p. 2164]. @mortelmans2024peatland, working with the peatland-specific land surface model PEATCLSM, instead "matched the temporal cumulative density functions (CDFs) of the PEATCLSM output variables" to those of the moisture codes in each grid cell [@mortelmans2024peatland, p. 448]. That step kept the percentile of a day fixed within the matching period, and so the counts above percentile thresholds, while leaving the absolute counts to move. It was the same split between the two threshold families reported here. A historical trend re-expressed in the new system's units should therefore be recomputed over the whole record rather than joined across the change, and reported with its metric family.

In 2024, the introduction to a joint special issue on good modelling practice named a last phase, model perpetuation, for models that support "ongoing decision making or operational processes" [@jakeman2024normalizing, p. 3]. The phase included "ensuring that plans and mechanisms are in place for appropriately monitoring, maintaining and updating the model" [@jakeman2024normalizing, p. 3]. @jakeman2024normalizing [p. 3] judged that existing suggestions of good practice "tend to focus on the model set up (phase 3), whereas the other phases are at least equally important". Their conclusion named "a next crucial step", the "more thorough justification of decisions, wherever possible stating the comparative effect of decision options on the outcomes of the modeling" [@jakeman2024normalizing, p. 11]. The 2025 revision updated a model in operational use, and the three series stated that effect for two decision options an agency faced, the version and the input resolution.

## Limitations

```{r}
#| label: limits-compute
#| output: false
# The quantitative limits statement. For each metric the minimum detectable trend
# is the slope this record could resolve at 90 per cent power, given the residual
# spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line. Expressing it over the whole
# window rather than per season is what makes it legible: a slope of 0.3 days per
# season is 10 days over 34 seasons, and the second number is the one a reader can
# judge.
lim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, trends$metric), function(d) {
  mdt <- median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    `Median observed slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Minimum detectable slope` = round(mdt, 3),
    `Minimum detectable change over the window` =
      round(mdt * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    `Observed change over the window` =
      round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE) * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
lim <- lim[order(match(lim$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(lim) <- NULL
write.csv(lim, file.path(outputs, "detectability.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
# How many metrics moved by less over the window than the record could detect.
n_below <- sum(abs(lim[["Observed change over the window"]]) <
                 lim[["Minimum detectable change over the window"]])
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-limits
#| tbl-cap: "What a window of this length can and cannot resolve. The minimum detectable slope is the trend at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 would reach 90 per cent power given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator relative to least squares and inflated for lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals. A metric whose observed change is smaller than its minimum detectable change is not evidence of no trend; it is evidence that this record cannot see one of that size."
fmt_tbl(lim)
```

@tbl-limits gave the quantitative form of what this study could not say. A null result and an underpowered result looked identical in a table of p values and were different claims. The median observed change over the window was smaller than the minimum detectable change in `r if (n_below == nrow(lim)) paste("all", nrow(lim)) else paste(n_below, "of the", nrow(lim))` metrics.

The study covered only the Canadian part of one basin, so whether the version effect had the same size elsewhere was untested. The study detected change and did not attribute it, because attribution required a comparison against a world without anthropogenic forcing, the human contribution to climate change [@kirchmeieryoung2019attribution, p. 4]. Four further limits applied to the absolute trends and not to the comparison between series, because whatever moved one series moved all three. No index of the El Niño Southern Oscillation or the Pacific Decadal Oscillation entered any model. A window that began and ended in different phases of those oscillations therefore biased the absolute trends. The sensor history of the stations was not available. At 75 airport stations across Canada, @vanwijngaarden2005examination found that replacing the psychrometer by the dewcel "produced a decreasing step in relative humidity at a number of stations" [@vanwijngaarden2005examination, p. 1]. Fuel typing did not vary through time, so a danger effect was not distinguished from fuel accumulation. The fixed window from 1 May to 30 September could not register a season that lengthened at either end. If the true season lengthened, trends in window counts understated trends in the season.

A year-round climate station of the kind @hanes2020overwinter used would recover the season from this basin. It would also allow the Drought Code to be overwintered rather than restarted each spring. @mcelhinny2020era5 showed that the restart changed the count of spread days.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

```{r}
#| label: conclusions-numbers
#| output: false
# The numbers the conclusions rest on, pulled from the objects above rather than
# retyped. A missing object stops the render rather than printing a hedge.
c_days_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
c_pct_gap <- 100 * c_days_gap / d_s1
c_dur <- ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S3", ct$Series)] -
  ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S2", ct$Series)]
stopifnot(length(c_dur) == 1, is.finite(c_dur))
c_abs_rate <- sc["migration, absolute", "rate"]
c_rel_rate <- sc["migration, relative", "rate"]
# The verdict as a sentence of its own, under the same five conditions the
# Results chunk scores, so the conclusion cannot assert a pattern the rates do
# not show.
c_verdict <- if (!is.finite(c_abs_rate) || !is.finite(c_rel_rate)) {
  "The divergence could not be scored."
} else if (c_abs_rate == 0 && c_rel_rate == 0) {
  "Divergence appeared under neither scheme, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism."
} else if (c_abs_rate > c_rel_rate) {
  "That was the pattern the mechanism predicted."
} else if (c_abs_rate > 0) {
  "Divergence appeared under both schemes, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism."
} else {
  "Divergence appeared under the percentile scheme alone, the opposite of the pattern the mechanism predicted."
}
# When nothing diverged, one sentence says so; otherwise the two rates and the
# verdict are printed in full.
c_migration <- if (is.finite(c_abs_rate) && is.finite(c_rel_rate) &&
                   c_abs_rate == 0 && c_rel_rate == 0) {
  "The migration changed no estimated trend at any station under fixed or percentile thresholds, which the design had set as a refutation of the mechanism."
} else {
  sprintf("The migration changed the estimated trend at %.0f per cent of station-metric combinations under fixed thresholds and at %.0f per cent under percentile thresholds. %s",
          c_abs_rate, c_rel_rate, c_verdict)
}
```

Over `r n_seasons` seasons in the Okanagan basin, the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System was run in both versions, FWI1987 and FWI2025, on one record. Slopes were positive in `r tr_up` of `r tr_n` station, series and metric combinations, and `r tr_sig` passed the corrected test. Of those, `r sig_station[[1]]` were at `r station_prose(top)`, which also rose relative to `r c("none", "one", "two", "three")[length(nb_up) + 1]` of its three neighbours. The 2025 report gave a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 as its example of continuity. That threshold selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(c_days_gap))` `r if (c_days_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under FWI2025 on hourly weather than under FWI1987, a change of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(c_pct_gap))` per cent. `r c_migration` The refutation extended down to a slope divergence of about `r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` days over the window, the resolution of this record. The three fuel moisture codes and the spread index, recomputed under the 2025 equations, shifted in level, `r slow_phrase`. `r if (n_excl_new == 0) "In no case did they change a trend this record could resolve" else sprintf("They changed a trend in %d of their slope differences", n_excl_new)`.

Fire danger trends should therefore be reported as days above a percentile of the series itself, not as counts above a fixed danger class. The percentile moved with its distribution across the version change and the class boundary did not. A count series joined across the change would carry a step of `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(shift$migration[1]))` days per season, which a fitted line read as a trend of `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(step_slope))` days per season. The reference period should be stated and fixed, with the base-period bias corrected where the record runs beyond it. The recommendation rested on the level result in one basin, and the study attributed no change to a cause. For daily ignition counts the three series were close to interchangeable. On the burning window the observed hourly weather and the reconstructed diurnal curve disagreed by `r sprintf("%.1f", c_dur)` hours per day. An agency migrating to FWI2025 on a 13:00 observation alone would inherit that difference with no sign of it in the output.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="docx"}

# Station-days are counted once, not once per component compared: the rows

op_n <- max(tapply(opc$n, opc$component, sum))
bias_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)

r_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n)

bui_bias <- bias_of("BUILDUP_INDEX")

The FWI2025 calculation used the Canadian Forest Service reference implementation [@nrcan2026cffdrsng] unmodified. The hourly record was retrieved from the BC Wildfire Service Weather Data Mart, whose FTP server the Service states "will be reaching the end of it's lifespan by January 2027" [@bcws2026datamart].
